utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, December 3rd, 2008, and I welcome our witness, first and foremost; and then I also welcome the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, and everyone helping us. Witness, could you please give me your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sulejman Tihic, the 26th of November, 1951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are born November 26th, 1951. So you were born on November 26th, 1951. Can you tell me, what is your occupation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I am the deputy speaker of the Chamber of Nations of the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm president of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in this court; and if so, can you tell us which case, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I testified several times: The first time in Mr. Tadic's case; the second time in the case against Blagoje Simic, or, rather, the Samac group; and the third time in the case against Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you testifying for the Prosecution or the Defence in these three cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Let me give you some details. I'm sure they won't surprise you, since you've already testified a number of times in this Tribunal, over several days, so you know exactly how things happen here. You will be asked questions by the representatives of the OTP, and you must answer these questions. These questions will be put to you based on the statement that you made at the OTP, and I believe that the OTP will also submit some documents to you. And during your proofing session yesterday with the Prosecution, you must have looked through a number of documents also. Then after this first phase, Mr. Seselj, the accused in these proceedings, will also put questions to you, and that will be the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj, being self-represented, as the late-Milosevic did, he will be directly asking questions to you. The three Judges on the Bench in front of you will also be asking questions in order to shed light on a number of items or to bridge some gaps that they may discover in some events. Try to be extremely brief and very concise in your answers. But given your background, I'm absolutely sure, yes, you will be very concise. If you don't understand a question, just ask the person putting the question to you to reformulate it, even if it's a Judge. Sometimes Judges don't formulate their questions extremely well, so that can happen, so just ask for reformulation. We have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half; but if you feel ill at ease and you want a break, just raise your hand and we'll allow you a break. The Prosecution has two hours for its examination-in-chief, Mr. Seselj has two hours for the cross-examination, so it's almost sure that we'll have to continue tomorrow. I'm sure that you made the necessary arrangements so that you could stay until tomorrow. So in a nutshell, that's how the hearing is going to occur, and I hope it will run smoothly. I welcome our representative of the OTP. He's ready, he's got his lectern. So now, Mr. Mussemeyer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. I want to start directly with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tihic, could you describe for us your professional background. Did you study; and if so, when and where? What was your occupation later on?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary and secondary school in Bosanski Samac. I graduated from law school at the University of Sarajevo. After I passed the Bar exam, I was elected judge at the municipal court at Bosanski Samac. After that, I was prosecutor for Madrica, Bosanski Samac, and Odzak. After that, I worked as a lawyer for nine years. After the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, for a while I worked at the embassy in Bonn as a councillor there, and after that in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. After that, I was vice-president of the SDA. I won in the election of 2002, and I was elected a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, I held the office of deputy speaker and speaker of the Chamber of Nations of the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am the president of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, the largest party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have been that since 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. Could you please explain us if you have already been engaged in politics before the outbreak of the conflict; and if so, in which party?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: At that time -- or, rather, before the democratic changes, I was, like many others, a member of the League of Communists, just an ordinary member. At the same time, I was socially active by being president of the Local Commune in Samac, also president of the Firefighting Association of Bosanski Samac. Before the first democratic elections, I joined the Party of Democratic Action. I was elected a member -- a councilman of the Assembly of Municipality of Bosanski Samac. After that, I elected the president of the Municipal Organisation of Bosanski Samac, and a member of the main board of the SDA party for all of Yugoslavia. What happened afterwards is what I've already told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you also have a position in the Doboj region?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I was vice-president of the Regional Board of the SDA for the region of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Given your position and your function today, I think you are in a position to tell us a bit more about the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and for that reason. I would like to introduce a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call up Exhibit number 140 on the Exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, I would like you to have a look on this document, when it shows up, and comment on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is a well-known map. It tentatively reflects the ethnic structure of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina; although, perhaps, if somebody is totally unfamiliar with the facts, it might seem that Bosnia-Herzegovina is divided along national or ethnic lines. However, that is not the case. Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, the ethnic structure of its population is such that it is mixed. Where you see the colour green here, denoting the Bosniak Muslims, and the colour red, depicting the Serbs, and blue, Croats, there were still representatives of many other ethnic groups or other nations in those areas. There are very few municipalities where one particular ethnic group dominated over the other. If we look at this map, it is a fact that there are some small deviations; for example, look at Banja Luka. Banja Luka is depicted as if its population is -- or, rather, that it's population was 50 per cent Serb in 1991. Serbs, Bosniaks, and Croats were there roughly in equal numbers, around 30 per cent. Perhaps there could have been a bit more Croats or a bit more Serbs, but I'm not sure about that. At any rate, that's what it was like, and it was similar in other towns. Because in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for centuries in all towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a coexistence between Catholic churches and mosques, and Orthodox churches, and synagogues. The population looked like a leopard skin, as it were. It wasn't like this, just red, just blue, just green. It was all mixed, all of it was mixed, up until the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: But as this map is based on the population census of 1991, could you say if the colours are correct, as they reflect the regions?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly, yes. I mentioned Banja Luka a moment ago. I don't think that colour is not exactly right. I don't think it was 50 per cent Serb. Possibly there was a Serb majority, but not around 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecution had to give us a survey of the population in accordance with the census of 1991, not to put this map here and to have the witness speculate. The fact that he's asking the witness to speculate is -- means there is no probative value involved in this whatsoever. We have to look at the results of the census for Banja Luka and then to see exactly what the figures were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I heard what you were saying, and it seems that the chart we have on the screen reflects the 1991 census, but the criteria used is a 50 per cent majority. You told us, and it was quite interesting, you told us that according to you, the colours don't really reflect the fact that in some areas, there were minorities; and as you said, it would be more accurate to see a leopard skin, in your words. So, according to you, don't you think that such a map should have different colours that could stress the ethnic majorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that should have been done from the very outset. You know, in addition to having a dominant colour, other colours should be represented on a particular surface, other ethnic groups, other national groups, because that would reflect the true situation. In this way, there was this politicization, as if some areas were Serb, Croat or Bosniak, which was not a good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. All this is on the record. Now please continue, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The intention of the Prosecution is to use this map to give a rough overview to assist the Judges in their findings later on, so this is the reason I would ask to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document shall be given Exhibit number P669. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, on this map, I see that this map was drafted by the OTP, by the Demographics Unit of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, it's written in the footnote, and it is based on the results of the census of 1991, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to continue with the next map. This is a map for Bosanski Samac. It has the 65 ter number 2579. Could you please call it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, I would like you to look at this map and comment on this.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, this is a map of the Posavina region; that is to say, a group of municipalities, so it's not only the municipality of Bosanski Samac. The municipality of Bosanski Samac is here in the middle and is shown in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Would you show us if Sagrina [phoen], for example --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Why are some names blackened out in this map? We see that names of many places have simply been redacted, deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, there are black lines and it looks like some names have been crossed out, probably for a reason. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think the reason is that these municipalities or towns are not important for this case. All the municipalities or little villages around Bosanski Samac are mentioned here just to give a rough overview to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what is redacted here is also a town that is in Bosanski Samac, and that is why this explanation provided by the Prosecutor is not a truthful one. You see here, within the municipality of Bosanski Samac, a town or a village was blackened. I insist that the Prosecution give us a clean map without any redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give us the name of the municipality that was crossed out. Which one was omitted, Mr. Seselj? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that a municipality was omitted. We have the region of Posavina here on this map. That's what it was called. I can't remember now exactly. We see there the municipality of Bosanski Samac and surrounding municipalities, and then we see two, four, six, seven names of towns and villages that were blackened out by a magic marker. This is a mockery of the Prosecution case. And in Bosanski Samac, one particular name was redacted, too. Why? That is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, would you have a blank map without anything crossed out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have a map. I must only search it. Just give me a second. I think it's the map 2874 on the exhibit list, but I did not check this. But the reason for blackening out is that Bosanski Samac is a so-called removed municipality where the Prosecution is allowed only to lead pattern evidence, so we concentrated on the locations which are important for the indictment to show pattern evidence. But if the Judges and the accused insist, we have nothing to hide to show you the exact map of this region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Show us another map, please, with unredacted cities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... by the Prosecutor makes even less sense than the previous one. Bosanski Brod is still on the map, too, the utmost west, and then Dervent and so on. He did not provide an explanation as to why the names of some towns and villages close to Bosanski Samac and within the municipality of Bosanski Samac itself were crossed out with a magic marker. I don't think that you can accept nonsensical explanations provided by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have a new map. Mr. Prosecutor, we have a new map. Nothing is crossed out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I observe, Mr. President, that Crkvina was redacted on the previous map. I could not tell a few moments ago; I could not know everything by heart. Now I see that Crkvina was redacted, and Crkvina is mentioned in Mr. Tihic's statement. Why did the Prosecution cross this out? Are they trying to ambush me or anyone else in this way? Look, Crkvina is here in the center of this map, and it was deleted in the previous map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, we have a map with all municipalities with red dots. Fine. Given the objections, do you still want to work with the first map, or can you work with the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have nothing against using the second map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Use the second, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, could you have a look on this and comment on this map?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This is a map of Bosanski Samac, and we see here the contours of the neighbouring municipalities. We have all the villages here that were referred to. We have the village of Crkvina, where the mass crime occurred. I don't know what else you would be interested in. I can explain all of this, of course. I know the territory of Samac very well. I practiced law there, and I went to all these different villages and I socialised with people. I went hunting and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, just one little thing for clarification on the map. It looks as if the area north of the river is just blank, and my question to you is: Did the village of Bosanski Samac stretch over to the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up here is the Sava River. On the other side of the Sava River is the Republic of Croatia. There was another village on the other side called Slavonski Samac. Administratively and politically, it was not linked to Bosanski Samac. It belonged to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, this map is labelled "Bosanski Samac." I would like to know whether the entire green area corresponds to the administrative municipality of Bosanski Samac or whether the Bosanski Samac municipality is only the red dot, or the yellow area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The colour yellow denotes the town only; whereas, the municipality of Bosanski Samac is all the rest, and these red dots are different villages and local communes in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, now I want to come to the situation before the outbreak of the war. Can you please roughly describe to us the ethnic distribution and the different ethnicities living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Bosanski Samac, the ethnic composition was approximately as follows: 44 per cent were Croats, 42 per cent were Serbs, about 7 per cent were Bosniaks, and then the rest were Yugoslavs and others. In the town of Bosanski Samac itself, the ethnic composition was somewhat different because the Bosniaks were predominant there, and then Serbs, and then Croats. The villages were mostly mono-ethnic, and the town had a mixed population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how was the relationship between these different ethnicities before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, inter-ethnic relations were always good. We lived together. We visited each other when religious holidays occurred in any one of the communities. I regularly went to Christmas celebrations, patron saints celebrations; and then on the occasion of Bajram, others would come to see me. The president of the SDS and the president of the HDZ visited me on the 6th of April for the Bajram holiday, and Bosanski Samac was attacked only on the 17th of April. According to what people told us as to what happened during the Second World War, in Bosanski Samac, the relations that prevailed were rather good as opposed to other areas. We lived together, we socialised. We respected one another. I'm convinced that not only in Bosanski Samac, but primarily in Bosanski Samac and throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, there never would have been a conflict between the Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks had there not been an intervention from the outside. That's the way it was through history, as an effect of world wars, regional conflicts, or direct interference from neighbouring countries. Even after this war, I've been going to Bosanski Samac very often. My child lives in Bosanski Samac, my grandchildren live in Bosanski Samac. I see that this tolerance and coexistence is being restored, and I hope that that will be the case in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, obviously there existed also a council of security in Bosanski Samac. Can you confirm this, and who was the member, and what was the goal of this council?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, in all the municipalities throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I do believe in other republics as well, there were security councils and councils for defence. These were the two most important bodies of every assembly, and it was made up mostly of respected citizens, politicians of the day. They discussed security situations at their meetings prior to the events; crime, public law and order, things like that; if there was some internal enemy or external enemy as was referred to at those times. And, mostly, at the period that we're discussing, we dealt with trying to avoid an inter-ethnic clash and conflict. We tried to solve various situations of various incidents and see that rumours weren't spread about or fears, to allay fears, and things like that. We tried to convince people that the situation should remain calm and conflict should be avoided. That was our goal. But nobody asked us much. Had people asked us in Samac, I'm quite sure that no conflict would have taken place. It all came from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the 1990s, obviously political parties have been founded. Can you tell us if this is true, and which parties were that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a time of the first multi-party democratic elections, as we referred to them at that time. Parties were set up as branches or departments of the parties that had already been formed at a republican level -- or, rather, at the level of the state. So in addition to the previous League of Communists that existed, the Serbian Democratic Party was set up, and the Party of Democratic Action, the Croatian Democratic Union, the Reformist Party, the Liberal Party, and so on and so forth. The HDZ, SDS, and SDA were treated as being national ethnic parties, parties of those particular nations and ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a short question for you, Witness. You are saying that everything came from outside. What do you mean by that? When you say "from outside," as opposed to the former Yugoslavia, or do you mean "from outside" as opposed to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Externally in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mostly, it came from Belgrade, from the Serb side, that is; the JNA or centres of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the parties, and did they have a common goal?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, relations were quite proper, good relations, and the aim was to replace the communists, to seize power from the communists, and to resolve certain ethnic questions along the way. However, as time passed and as the situation throughout Yugoslavia deteriorated, we began discussing general questions more and discuss local questions less, and the differences at a general level between the parties, and these were reflected at a local level as well. We went further and further into the realm of division, and differences came to the fore. The Serb side wanted to retain Yugoslavia at all costs, the kind of Yugoslavia that would have a unitarian character with a strong centralised power and authority. The SDA and the HDZ were in favour of a different kind of Yugoslavia. The HDZ was in favour of a greater degree of independence and autonomy and full independence ultimately. The SDA wanted to retain Yugoslavia as a form of confederation or federation or staggered confederation. We were conscious of the fact that Bosniaks, as a nation and as an ethnicity, did not have the strength and power to confront the other side, and that they would be the biggest victims. President Izetbegovic did all he could took retain Yugoslavia and to prevent conflicts of that kind from taking place. So together with the President Gregoric of the Macedonia, he proposed various forms of confederation and federation and to preserve Yugoslavia as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there also been a TO unit in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, in addition to the armed forces or, rather, the JNA, you have the system of territorial defence; and, for the most part, that system came under the power and authority of the republics. Each municipality had its own Territorial Defence Staff, and then there was the Territorial Defence Staff in the republic. There was one in Samac and one in Sarajevo, which was the Republican Staff. Those staffs had their units, they had their weapons. At sometime, I think it was in 1990, that pursuant to a decision by the JNA or some state organ, the weapons were taken away from the Territorial Defence and moved to JNA depots and warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been founded a special unit in Bosanski Samac at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence Staff was formed, but it wasn't really working. Then the Republican Staff of Territorial Defence appointed a new commander and a new chief, Bozanovic Marko, and I think Alija Fitozovic was the second man. They started putting the documents in order, bringing data and information up to date, and then Samac was on the agenda. But, actually, it never -- it was never operational in the proper sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: As far as I'm informed, there was founded a unit which got a number. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was a unit that was established by the JNA. I was in that unit -- or, rather, a garrison of the JNA from Brcko was set up, and it was called the 4th Detachment, I think, of the 17th Tactical Group, something like that. That unit numbered about 400 men, mostly Serbs, but there were Bosniaks and Croats among them, too. They were issued quite a lot of weapons, heavy weapons, well, for that time, and they had automatic rifles, machine-guns, cannons, hand-held launchers and so on. This gave rise to a lot of unrest in the town, and they were under the direct command of the JNA, that detachment, I mean; although, they were made up of civilians, and civilians of Bosanski Samac. A lot of those civilians had been in the army previously, or in the police force, or in the security services generally. So the detachment was formed of their family members, too, close relations, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What reason was given to found this 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason that was publicly bandied about was that the detachment was there to prevent inter-ethnic clashes and to eliminate any attempts that might be made on the part of the paramilitaries to attack Bosanski Samac, including certain units from Croatia which could possibly attack Bosanski Samac. That was what the public was told, so that some people, believing that to be true, joined up, joined the detachment, people who believed that Yugoslavia could be preserved and who believed in the Yugoslav People's Army as being a joint army of all the peoples and citizens of the country. However, in reality, things were quite different. That detachment, and we found that to be true when the attack on Bosanski Samac was launched, was to prolong the politics and policies of Belgrade and Greater Serbia, and with the other units took part in the occupation of Bosanski Samac, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. Mr. Registrar, I would like to show to the witness now the document with the number 996, 65 ter number 996. This is a decision on the establishment of the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And when it shows up, I would like, Mr. Tihic, you to read until the first sentence of paragraph 2 -- of Article 2. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, there must be a mistake in the transcript. The number indicated is 966 and not 996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's true. It was vice versa; it's 996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends how you read it, of course. 996. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, could you please read until the first sentence of Article 2?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. You want the first sentence: "On the basis of Article 256 of the [indiscernible] BiH and from the area of Bosanski Samac, Gradacac, Orasje, and Odzak, which was expressed at the referendum held on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991, and pursuant to the decision on the establishment of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 29th of February, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People adopted the decision on the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac and the Serbian municipality of Pelagicevo, in the process of being established. "Article 1. The Serbian municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo shall be established. The seat of the municipality shall be in Bosanski Samac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And the first sentence of Article 2, please, also.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: "The Serbian municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo shall comprise the following settlements: Bosanski Samac ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. I wanted to stop here. Do you know this decision, and what is your comment about this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that decision, and my comment is that the decision is contrary to the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. It was established bypassing the regular procedure on the establishment of municipalities, because as you can see here, they sat down and decided that, and it was only the deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party; that is to say, one party made this decision, plus some other deputies from some other parties that wanted to come. But we don't see any deputies from Croatia, or other Bosniaks, or other ethnic group, for that matter. So a decision of that kind was not legally valid. It was just a contribution to the clashes and divisions. And as you can see here, they changed the names -- place names, and added Serbian in front: "Serbian Gradacac," "Srpski" -- "Srpska Korenica," "Srpska Ledenica," and so on and so forth, "Srpska Slenje [phoen]," "Slatina." None of these places existed with the word "Srpski," "Serbian," in front, so there was no -- this could not be done lawfully. They encroached upon our territory, some local communities which were not exclusively made up of a Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, for once, we have a witness who's special insofar as you are a prominent political figurehead. You were a lawyer, you were a judge, and you were a prosecutor. So we have a lawyer in front of us. It hasn't escaped me that in this document, some municipalities were changed and the word "Serbian" was added on to them. But in looking at this text, we see that there is a special mention of Article 258 of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't have the constitutional text before me, but what does this Article 258 actually state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that that was the legal basis for establishing the municipalities; however, that was just a general legal premise, allowing for the formation of municipalities. And from those general legal conditions, you have the law on the territorial organisation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which provides for the exact conditions according to which individual municipalities may be set up. So this is just a general condition, and then the law goes on and stipulates the conditions and procedures under which this is to be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I think that the Prosecutor ought to show us this Article 258 of the Constitution to avoid speculation and suppositions on the part of the witness, and the Prosecution does possess the entire Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber can also look up Article 258, and I'm sure our legal officer is currently doing this. Irrespective of this, Witness, it seems that in this text, there is something unprecedented here, i.e., there is the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had a legal existence. But on the 29th of February, the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, even though the referendum had taken place, as the text states, on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991. There had also been the declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since you are a lawyer, according to you, which document should prevail in this matter? From what I understood, it was the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So please tell us, what is the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I want to say that this referendum that is referred to in the preamble of this decision was an unlawful referendum which was held on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991, and that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that decision, that it was the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina who declared it null and void. So that decision was not in keeping with the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina either. So the whole legal premise upon which this preamble is based was declared null and void by the Constitutional Court, and the decision was declared null and void. Now, the referendum on Bosnia's independence was on the 21st of February and the 1st of March, 1992, and that is something quite different and is not mentioned in this decision. Otherwise, no laws at the time or any laws now in Bosnia-Herzegovina allowed for municipalities to have any ethnic epithets, not Serbian, not Bosniak, not Croatian, so all these names that were with the epithet Serbians, Serbian Sarajevo, Serbian et cetera, et cetera, all these places, and Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina overthrew and declared null and void because they were deemed to be contrary to the Human Rights Declaration. And even today in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you can't name a place after an ethnic group, because that is contrary to the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights and Freedoms as well. So this decision is completely unlawful, completely illegal. It's just a group of people gathered together, proclaiming these municipalities and the Republic of the Serbian people. This was quite illegal, quite unlawful, and as I said, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina overthrew it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please read also Article 8 of this decision?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: "The official-som [as interpreted] workers and workers with special authority and workers in the organs of administration, organisations, institutions and funds, shall retain ..." Can you show the bottom of that? "... senior officials, management, and employees with special authority and employees of Serbian nationality in the administrative bodies, organisations, institutions, and funds, shall retain their posts, rights, and duties until the definitive distribution of assets has been determined ," which means that it speaks about Serbs again. Decisions like that were passed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all the members of other nations, other ethnic groups, that worked as employees, or in management, or whatever, remained without a job. They were dismissed. The only people retained were representatives of the Serbian people, and that is proof yet again of just how far this decision was unlawful, because this is what they wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give this document an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P670. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I would like to go now to the situation before the attack on Bosanski Samac. Had there been rumours spread in the village; and if so, what kind of rumours?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you about the situation in town, and I assume it was similar in the villages. But rumours did go round about an attack and the fact that Bosanski Samac, as a municipality and a town, would be taken over. The rumours were different, there were different rumours going around. They ranged from people saying that units of the Serbian Territorial Defence and JNA would come and take control of Samac; to the other end, that Croatian units that were stationed in Slavonski Samac would cross the river and take control of Bosanski Samac. The Serbs were afraid that this might be done from units -- by units from Croatia, taking into account the experience of Bosanski Brod. So those were their fears, and those were the information -- that was the information they had. Those were those rumours. We were afraid of both. We didn't want anybody to take control of Bosanski Samac, not the Croatian units, or the Serb units, or the JNA. We wanted Bosanski Samac to remain Bosnian and not belong to one ethnicity, neither the Serb nor Croatian ethnicity. But as I said, these rumours were very frequent, and we became accustomed to them. There were all kinds of rumours going around, and we thought nobody would be mad enough to attack and occupy Samac because that would mean war, that would mean suffering and casualties. But we got so used to hearing those rumours that we didn't attach the importance that we ought to have attached to them. We turned a blind eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you undertake something to organise a defence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, and I'm now speaking as a Bosniak: We were in the minority there in Bosanski Samac, about 7 per cent of us; and rumours kept reaching us that the Serbs were arming themselves, that the JNA had distributed weapons to them, as indeed it had, and that the Croatians were being armed through Croatia. What were we Muslim Bosniaks going to do? We'll be the victims in all of this. Then we started thinking about what we could to. We started organising ourselves, conscious of the fact that any organisation on our part would not be on a level with what the other ethnicities were doing, because they were far more numerous. I gave you the percentages earlier on; 45 per cent Croats, 42 per cent Serbs, and 7 per cent of Bosniaks. The Croats, in a way, relied on Croatia; the Serbs relied on the JNA; and what could we Bosniaks do, faced with a situation like that? But, anyway, we organised some guards that we set up at the entrance to Bosanski Samac to prevent any paramilitary units entering and causing mayhem, killing the population, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the document under 65 ter number 1117 to be shown on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, when you see this document, could you please tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This is a letter or a document sent to the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence; and, along with it, there was a list of all those who wished to be included into the defence of Bosanski Samac, because we, as Bosniaks, thought it was a good idea for the Territorial Defence Staff to function and that it should be a legal institution, without setting up any party, armies, or ethnic armies, or anything like that. I think you must have the list attached to this letter with the names of people who were ready to join the Territorial Defence Staff and act for it in Bosanski Samac. I think there might have been about 100 names on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: They are on the following pages, just for the information of the Judges. There you can see a list with many names. Mr. President, I would like to have this document moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe that this list should be shown. It is very important for the public, not just to be tendered into evidence. Let it be shown to the public that the list contains exclusively Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was the question I was going to put to you, if Mr. Seselj hadn't taken the floor. While you were answering the Prosecutor, I was reviewing this list. I note that there are 212 names on it. And unless I'm mistaken, we see the allocation of these people in several units, and you're number 1 on that list, and I see Brigade number 3. I took due note of the fact that there were 7 per cent Muslims, so you were a small minority, but you felt that you should set up an entirely Muslim TO. But you might tell us that there are also some Serbs and Croats in this list; I don't know. But tell us exactly how it came to be that in such a situation, with a 7 per cent minority, you can come up with an armed forces. So, please, first tell us whether these 212 people are all Muslims; and, secondly, tell us what was the purpose of the force that was to be set up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly, predominantly, there were Muslims, but there were also members of other ethnic groups. You can see and judge by their names, and people living in Bosnia can recognise Muslim names, names of Orthodox Christians and Catholics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several Croats, but I could not see a single Serb, judging by the names. If Mr. Tihic knows of a Serb there, he can name them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I continue my answer? We submitted a list of Bosniaks who were ready to join the Territorial Defence Staff, and the Staff comprised members of both Croat and Serb ethnic groups as well. We expected, on the part of Croats and Serbs, to provide lists containing thousands of people. We did not pretend for the Territorial Defence Staff to comprise only Muslims, because we were only 7 per cent of the population; and Serbs and Croats were supposed to submit their lists numbering 1.000, 2.000 names each. We could include on the list those citizens of the town of Bosanski Samac, who are predominantly Muslims, who contacted us and wanted to be made available; and we expected the Serbs and the Croats to submit more numerous lists because they were the majority peoples in that area-

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us whether there were any Serbs on this list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up a bit, please, so I can see the last page here. Let's go to the next page, please. Can we have the next page, please. Next page, please. Next page, please. Next page, please. I haven't recognised a single Serb name on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's give it a number. I believe Mr. Mussemeyer wanted to tender this document with the list. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P671. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one note. I believe it will be interesting and important that there are only six Croats on this list, out of 212, and not a single Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, could you please let us know if you and your neighbours realised a kind of strange behaviour of your Serb neighbours at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Strange? Well, there were divisions opening up, generally speaking, concerning the preservation of Yugoslavia. Those differences appeared. Strangely enough, over weekends, people would go back to their villages where they hailed from, out of fear, presumably, that somebody would attack the town of Samac, and different people had different information. They followed generally the policies created by the Serb leadership with respect to the future of the then and now ex-Yugoslavia. There was some of them who disagreed with such policies, who were concerned. One who told me, as a lawyer - he was a client - he told me that in the village of Batkusa, a helicopter of the JNA landed, carrying some special unit wearing red berets, and that those men were very -- treated the villagers of Batkusa very roughly. They beat up, allegedly, the Serb guards who were guarding against the Croatian village of Luka. Then after that both guards, Serbs and Croats, went to a cafe, and the Red Berets beat them up and cut their hair as punishment, allegedly, for drinking with the Croats instead of keeping guards against them. They also meted out rough treatment towards the women, and their arrival there was not met with general approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify. You mentioned that people were leaving the town on Friday. Who left the town on Friday, all the ethnicities or specific ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I do not remember Mr. Tihic saying that. I demand a the Prosecutor to cite the lines on the transcript, with regard to departures over weekends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I don't know what you say in your language, but you're not supposed to demand anything. You can request but don't demand, because in my own language, I had "demand," and you should only request. It might be a problem with the translation of the word you used in B/C/S. The interpreters are telling me that you did demand, but you're not supposed to demand. You can only request. Witness, regarding this weekend, the story of the weekend, maybe we got a little bit mixed up and I haven't really understood what you said. So please explain. Either the people working in your city were leaving for the villages because it was the weekend, and would come back with information; or those were people who were in the villages and, over the weekend, they came to the city maybe to do some shopping, and then would relate and relay rumours. So could you please explain what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually, over the weekend, inhabitants of Bosanski Samac of Croat and Serb ethnicity, who lived there in the town, would go to the villages, mono-ethnic villages, Serb or Croat, together with their families, out of fear that Bosanski Samac would be attacked either by the Croatian side or the Serbian side. Rumours would be spread before the weekend came, so-called confidential information; and people, out of fear of being there when either Serb or Croat units attacked, would go back to their villages, feeling more secure, and then would come back to the town of Bosanski Samac on Monday to go to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, it was during all this shuttling, tos and fros, that you heard that the Red Berets had come with helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a client in my office, law office, I found out that the Red Berets had arrived. That man spoke about that in confidence to me. I mentioned him. His name is in the record. I don't know whether I should repeat his name so that he could make -- have problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for this; however, this detail is very important. If the Red Berets did come with a helicopter from the JNA, this seems to demonstrate that the army does control this unit. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. The army controlled all those paramilitary units. Those were not paramilitary units; they were special units either of MUP of Serbia or of the JNA. They maybe were not officially labelled as such, but nobody else could have arrived on a JNA helicopter and have so much weapons. So these were special units operating pursuant to orders of either the police, the military, or security services; and they wore military uniforms with some other insignia other than that of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you say, I seem to understand that these Red Berets were special units of the army. That's what you seem to be saying, and they were not paramilitaries. But this is already a very important distinction. Then you also added a small detail, and you said that these units might have come from the MUP. The MUP is the Ministry of Interior, it's not the Ministry of Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, later I found out that those Red Berets were part of the MUP or Serbian police, police of the Republic of Serbia. At that moment, they wore military uniforms, so I thought they were part of the military. But after the war, I learned that the Red Berets had been part of the police of Serbia; and Zvezdan Jovanovic, the person who killed Prime Minister Djindjic, used to be in Bosanski Samac. He was the warlord there. He was the master of life and death. He mistreated people, looted whatever he could loot. At the time, he was a Serbian hero. But in reality, he was a criminal, and criminals do not have any nation or religious affiliation. Eventually, he killed a Serbian prime minister and was in Bosanski Samac during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you learned later on that these Red Berets reported to the MUP. But if Green Berets from the MUP are transported on board army helicopters, does this mean that the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Defence, regarding this special operation, were working in a coordinated fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, by all means; not only in that situation, but throughout the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They worked hand in hand together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to go a bit back in history just to follow the chronology. Mr. Witness, you already mentioned that weapons were distributed. To whom were they distributed, who did this, and did all the ethnicities get the weapons equally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: First of all, the JNA distributed the weapons; and mostly, almost exclusively, they distributed them to members of the Serb people, and their mobile units were mostly located in Serb villages in Bosanski Samac. And the 4th Detachment, which was in the town itself, some 400 people in all, 80 per cent of the composition were Serbs, 20 per cent were others; and the JNA distributed weapons to them, and some Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats got some of those weapons. We also tried to procure weapons, the Bosniaks. I presume that the Croats did so or tried to do so through Croatia. But what we did have was symbolic. I remember a case where we received from Croatia 50 assault rifles, automatic rifles; and I suggested that it be delivered to the Territorial Defence Staff and that they should sign a receipt in a legal and lawful manner and put some individuals in charge of those weapons, because I feared that weapons may be used in an unofficial capacity or for personal reasons, maybe in a cafe to settle an individual's cause. There was always this fear, because there were some weapons, like hunting rifles and automatic rifles, there was this fear for those weapons to be misused or to cause an incident. That's why we wanted the TO Staff to function, to be the lawful institution which would register all private weapons and put people in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What happened to the bridge in Bosanski Samac in the middle of April?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in mid-March, one month before the attack on Bosanski Samac, approximately, the bridge in Bosanski Samac was damaged by explosives. It wasn't completely destroyed, but it was damaged to the extent that no traffic could pass over it. It's difficult to say who did it. Some thought and spread rumours that the JNA did it, and the Serbs, some, said that it was done from the Croatian side. But the gist of the matter is that it didn't perform its functions. It would make more sense for the Serbs to have done that, because that bridge was used for illegal trafficking of weapons entering Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was logical for the Serb side to try to stem the flow of weapons into Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in other parts along the Sava, there had been some blowing up of the bridges, so the overall traffic was funneled through the Samac bridge and maybe another one in a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have the photo of 65 ter number 2235 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, does this depict the destroyed bridge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the bridge in Samac. This is the road traffic segment, and there was also the railway bridge, but it can't be seen on this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this photograph of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P672. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, before the outbreak of the conflict, did you realise the arrival of strangers to the village?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that. It could be seen in the streets. But primarily it was seen in the cafes, that people using the Ekavian dialect from Serbia were there and socialising with members of the 4th Detachment, and they were in civilian clothes, of course. I heard once that there were three people from the Croatian side who purported and introduced them as members of the HOS, H-O-S, but I think that was a single occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How did you personally experience the outbreak of the conflict? Please describe this to us.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: On that evening, I had some meetings. The atmosphere in the town was very tense. There were rumours that Samac was about to be attacked, and together with my wife from my house, and my brother with his wife, we transferred to our mother's house. And at around 2.00, intensive shooting started. Previously, there were instances of shooting, but this time around it lasted a long time. I looked out the window at one point, and I saw members of the 4th Detachment in the yard. There were some other units. That was around two or three. The members of my party came in a car and invited me to flee Bosanski Samac. I rejected that suggestion because I thought I should stay with my people to talk, to negotiate with the Serb side. I could not imagine what could happen. I did not have that experience at the time. Telephone communication was disrupted for a time, and phone lines were reconnected later on. In the morning, I called my neighbour of Serb ethnicity, suggesting that I transfer to his home. Given the situation, I had realised that Samac was occupied. Miso Pavlovic was that neighbour. I came to his place. His father and mother were there as well. We sat down, we talked. And at some other time Blagoje Simic, the president of the SDS, phoned. I tried to call -- talk to him in the way that we used to talk, to the effect that: "This all should stop. Let's sit down and agree." By that time, the paramilitaries reportedly had killed somebody in Mahala. I suggested to Blagoje, "Let's sit down," but he said, "There's no negotiations. We're at war. The Serbian people is at war with the Bosniaks, with the Croats. Surrender your weapons." I did not expect somebody who I had known to act in this way. We socialised, we had many contacts through political associations. Then my neighbour suggested I should go somewhere else, where I would be safer. I phoned my colleague, Borislav Pisarevic. He's a lawyer. We used to work at the Court together. He was the president of the Court; I was a judge there. We tried to arrange for my departure from Samac because I realised what a dangerous situation it was. Boro came in the afternoon. I was at my place with my wife. Boro tried to get into contact with Simo Zaric, who then was part of either police or military structures, I'm not sure which. But he could not reach him, which meant that I could not leave Samac. The following day, a member of Grey Wolves or some other unit from Serbia and a domestic policeman took Boro and me to police. The commander of the Serb police, Stevan Todorovic, waited for us next to the car. He was waving his gun and threatening both of us, asking Boro why he had provided sanctuary for me in his house. We went to the police station. They separated Boro and me, kept him black, or kept him "crni." They demanded that I went to the radio station and invite the citizens to surrender their weapons, to abstain from opening fire; although, nobody opened fire anymore, because that morning the few Bosnian Muslims who had weapons rounded up in the center of town and did not know what to do. I spoke on the phone with one of them, with Ibrahim Sakic, asking him what the situation was like. I said that I had been offered for the JNA to enter Bosanski Samac and guarantee peace. Ibrahim later spoke to Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic, one of the JNA commanders, and they surrendered their weapons. He walked in front of APCs, he knew who had weapons, and they went house by house and collected weapons. Some 20 people with rifles could not do anything against the 20 armoured vehicles that entered the town. So my appeal over the radio waves over Radio Samac would not serve any purpose because there was no resistance at that point in time, because the Serbian Territorial Defence, Chetnik detachments, the units from Serbia, the JNA, were overwhelming. I was beaten the first time when I was taken to the police station, before I was taken to the radio station. A person, Mirkovic, a.k.a. Lugar, beat me up. He came to me and asked me, "Who are you?" I said, "Sulejman Tihic, president of the SDA." He pretended not to hear, and as I came closer to him, he punched me in the stomach. I fell down, then people standing by kicked me. The person who was supposed to escort me to Radio Samac told them to stop. That person first took me to the radio station, where I read out an already-typed statement to the effect that I invited the citizens to surrender, to not open fire, and that it would be okay for the JNA to take control, or words to that that effect. I was then brought back to the police station, and there I was interrogated. That person, Lugar, beat up again. Some questions made no sense to the effect of "Who was in the leadership of the SDA." But that was a well-know fact; it wasn't confidential. I know that he phoned a friend in Valjevo over the phone and explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I'm sorry to interrupt. I think it's time for the break, and I will come back to this in more detail after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have something to deal with briefly before the break. May I? Mr. President, in the Serbian legal system, the accused can put forth requests and launch appeals. In the Serbian system, the accused person cannot beg anyone for anything, except for a partner amnesty later. I did not find anything in the Rules of The Hague Tribunal stating anything different. If ever I said "please," that just meant it is an ingrained part of my personality to be considerate and well-mannered. But if ever I said the word "please," or words to that effect, or "I beg you," I will never do that again, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the Serbian system, this is the International Tribunal, and it operates with its own special rules. There are requests. You cannot demand. There are no demands. We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Before we resume, Mr. Mussemeyer, I shall give the witness Article 258 in B/C/S, and I will ask him to read it because we haven't found an English version of this. We have this document, and I shall ask the witness to read out Article 258, and the interpreters can translate it. Usher, would you mind giving this document to the witness, please. Witness, I'm going to ask you to work a little bit. I'll ask you to read Article 258, and the interpreters will translate this for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Organisations of Associated Labour, self-management interest communities, and other self-management organisations and communities have the right and responsibility to take part actively in the defence of the country; and in relation to that, organise and carry out preparations, ensure resources, and carry out other tasks that are of interest for national defence, in accordance with the Constitution, law, plans, and decision of social-political communities. These organisations and communities are responsible for carrying out these tasks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for having read this article, which seems to grant a number of entities a responsibility in defence matters. Do you have anything to add to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, the wrong paragraph was referred to, in terms of this decision. It doesn't have to do with the territorial organisation of the republic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, you now had occasion to convince yourself of what this looks like when one deals with assumptions in the courtroom. On the basis of this article of the Constitution, a newly-established municipality indicates its rights in the sphere of national defence, and this was not used as legal grounds for establishing a new municipality, by breaking up existing municipalities. This was an arbitrary interpretation in the courtroom that was blessed, as it were, by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the article has been translated, it's on the record, the witness has provided us with his comment, and Mr. Seselj his position. Let's resume now. Mr. Mussemeyer, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I want to come back to the night when the conflict started. You told us that you got telephone calls. Do you remember getting a telephone call from Muslim members of the 4th Detachment, and what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you are referring to. What telephone call; on the eve of the attack on Samac, or after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: During this attack, you were at a meeting, and during this meeting, you got telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody phoned on the eve of the meeting that was held in the evening in Bosanski Samac, the night before Samac was to be attacked; and that is when someone from the ranks of my supporters from the SDA, a citizen, called me and said somewhere on the outskirts of Bosanski Samac, near the railway station, that there were soldiers there in military uniforms. I took that as one of the series of information that we were receiving every day, especially in the evening. And, as time went by, I stopped attaching any particular importance to this information. Sometimes, this information would prove to be wrong. Sometimes, it proved to be truth that some units, indeed, had entered, but then they would leave. So I did take note of that, but I did not take any steps, except for providing information further on. I don't know if I could have taken any steps or done anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you get any information that people were killed at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The following day when Samac was attacked, then I referred information to the effect that in Donja Mahala, in that part of town, these paramilitary specialists, as we called them, had already started killing people. Yes, that is the information I received. That was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was the name of the unit or of the units these soldiers belonged to mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that they then mentioned that these were Arkan's men or Grey Wolves. For us, all of these who were coming from Serbia, these specials, we called them "specials," we called them "the multi-coloured ones." Arkan was a big thing for all of them, so then all of these units were called "Arkan's men," or "The Grey Wolves" sometimes, because people knew they existed, too; that is to say, they were not regular JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the expression "Seselj's men" was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, the term "Chetniks" was used, you know. I remember, when they brought me to the police station, there were different uniforms there. Then also I saw those Chetniks with those beards and fur hats, as if they came out of the movies we used to watch from the Second World War, and I thought, my god, is this a dream or is this really happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since you are present today, I can ask you the following question. I believe you can answer this question. A while ago, you said that there were Arkan's men, paramilitary units, and so on and so forth. How is it that an army like the JNA, that had a well-established, worldwide reputation, did not have its own units, its own special units, like some armies in the world have, and had rather resort to units like Arkan's units? Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, the then-JNA had lost its commander. The Presidency of the SFRY, as a collective organ, could not reach consensus, agreement, with regard to many questions, including defence questions. Then the JNA was led by commanders who were predominantly of Serb ethnicity; and, most probably, the president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, exerted an influence, a real influence. He had a true and real influence and power. In my view, this was a combination between the military and these units that were trained either within the scope of the military or the police, who wore green military uniforms. And in addition to JNA officers in the field, they were commanded by somebody else from Belgrade, from these intelligence circles, from the intelligence community. Now, why the JNA allowed itself that kind of thing, well, because the JNA had lost its commander. Then the commanders in the military started conducting the defence and saying what was allowed and what was not allowed. I mean, they lost their civilian commander. That is what I've been trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, according to you, this is due to the fact that the JNA was no longer headed by a commander. That's why the generals, according to what you are saying, that had lower ranks managed the situation in this manner, and this is why these units were established. Your explanation is an interesting one and, of course, requires scrutiny on the part of the Bench. I have another issue in the same line I would like to put to you. We have been told, and the accused Seselj told us this during one of his many cross-examinations of a number of witnesses, that people mistrusted the JNA. There was a degree of mistrust because JNA symbolized communism. Since the JNA found it difficult to recruit soldiers, the law entitled volunteers to not be incorporated in the JNA, but the volunteers could, nonetheless, take part in defence operation of the fatherland. This was based on a voluntary basis, and this was enshrined in the law. We actually saw the text relating to that. Now, you, yourself, in your municipality which you had the honour of presiding at some point, did you feel that there was such a hostility vis a vis the JNA, whatever the ethnicity might be, whether it be Croats, Muslims, or Serbs, vis a vis these volunteers? What do you feel about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that as far as Bosniaks and Croats are concerned, that they primarily viewed the JNA as a Serb army because the command was Serb; and I don't think there were problems, especially as far as Serbs were concerned, to have this army manned in the regular way in accordance with the law. I think that these volunteer units are a consequence of the political situation in the country, and that they were created by the intelligence services that were supposed to do this dirty part of the job; namely, to come in before the JNA, to commit crimes. Then after that, the JNA shows up as some kind of saviour and then again they leave, and leave the matter to local Serb units and these paramilitaries. These paramilitary units, well, I don't think that they are classical volunteers. I think that there were quite a few mercenaries there, criminals. We see how they behaved. We see the killings, the abuse, the looting. I remember that some of them came to Samac, and they claimed that they had been in prison. I know that some men from Samac who had been in prison, in the special units they found their old prison mates. So these were not traditional volunteers who had come to fight for the freedom of their country. There was lots of crime involved there and a lot of criminals. Time did show that they were not patriots or nationalists. They were criminals, ultimately. I mentioned Zvezdan Jovanovic, who for a while could have looked like some kind of a patriot or some kind of a hero, national hero, and then he proved to be a criminal. We, however, in Samac knew that straight away, because they were stealing vehicles, printing false driving licenses and traffic licenses. They were killing, beating people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, from what you've just told us, I have the feeling that there are three key moments. The first one is when the intelligence services, according to what you are saying, instrumentalised a number of individuals who will then, in a particular area, commit crimes and abuses. That is the first key moment. In the second key moment, the JNA steps in, establishes law and order, and then leaves. The third key moment is when the paramilitary units remain where they are and will then also commit abuses. Have I summed up what you have said correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, except for the third matter. Along with the paramilitaries, the Serb units stayed behind of the Serb Territorial Defence, so they were there together. The paramilitaries remained, they were still dominant, and they were the masters of life and death. They were the ones who were killing, looting, and who, inter alia, had as one of their objectives a disruption of inter-ethnic relations, so that they would drag other members of their ethnic group into the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I would like to come back to the situation after you gave the interview. You were brought back to the police station, and you told us already that you have been heavily beaten by a certain Lugar. Do you remember a beating where Lugar was making telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. He made a telephone call. I realised that he was speaking to a woman, and she asked him where he was, and he said, "Well, I'm working, and you see how I'm working." Then he turned the receiver towards me, and then this colleague of his would hit me, then I would moan, so that she would hear through the receiver how he was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you ever been beaten by people originating from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, never. The Serbs from Bosanski Samac never beat me. If they could, they helped me, you know. When those specials, these paramilitaries as you call them - I think that that is a term that is completely wrong - when they would go out, then the commander of the police station, who was a Serb, then he'd bring a doctor to see me. He'd give me some food to eat, he'd give me lemonade, he'd let me go to the toilet, which meant a lot, you know. While I was there, they never beat me. The local Serbs from Bosanski Samac never beat me. You know, I knew all them, they knew me, they knew their father, they knew my grandfather. I also knew them. Very often, they would even apologise to me when they had to take me out, when these people would beat me, and they'd say, "Doctor, sorry," because there was this custom in Samac that a lawyer would be called "Doctor."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When the beatings stopped or the interrogations stopped, where have you been brought?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You see, I was taken away that evening first to the Staff of the Territorial Defence. This is opposite to the police station. It was like a warehouse, say 15 metres by 20 metres. There were already about 50 persons there, and, of course, all of it started. We had to sing Chetnik songs. They beat us indoors, outdoors. There were all sorts of interrogations, senseless ones, just for the sake of the beatings. All night, this went on. There was a concrete floor, and they gave us these pieces of cardboard to sort of lie down, but, I mean, you couldn't lie down because somebody would walk in all the time. Someone would walk in and say, "I'm one of Arkan's men, and I'm a person belonging to this or that unit." I don't know whether that was true or not. Then, according to their own criteria, whenever they take someone out, whether they liked this person, didn't like the person, beat them, and then they'd force us to sing their songs, louder, louder, and even louder. You couldn't sing any louder. Later on, people of Samac said this could be heard to the center of town and throughout town. We had to sing these songs so loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe to us in detail what Lugar exactly did to you and how he beat you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him a few times, if I can put it that way. Before I went to Radio Samac, when I came to the building - when I returned from Radio Samac, that is - I told you that a moment ago, when he was talking to someone out there in Serbia. Then once, when a Serb soldier got killed. Now, was he killed by the HVO? I mean, well, then he beat me up, too. I was in the police building then, and the room was, say, 2 metres by 1.20 metres. There were about nine of us there, and there was a bench there, and we were there for about a week. You slept there, you sat there on that bench. You couldn't go to the toilet. You may go to urinate, but then they beat you black and blue on the way. But they didn't allow us to pass a stool. That's how the days went by. I remember that Lugar would come in, I remember that he had these grenades, and he'd say, "I've just come from the funeral of this Serb soldier, and I swore at his grave that I would take my revenge." He looked at this cell. There were nine of us there, and he said, "President," and I was the president of the SDA and that's how he knew me, and he said, "President, you're going to be last."
