Then he took these men out one by one and he beat them, one, two, three, five blows, and then he returned that person. Then, finally, my turn came. I thought that he'd kill me because he said that he'd be taking his revenge, and I was the last one. There was this hall in front of these cells. Perhaps it was four or five metres long. Then, as he would hit me, it was like a boxer's blow and I would fall down, but I'd have to get up straight away, because if I wouldn't get up, then he would trample me with his feet, and then again and again and again. I don't know how many times this happened. And, finally, when I could no longer get up, I was lying down there, and then he jumped onto my chest, and I put my hands up this way and I heard something break. I tried to protect myself with my hands, and then he said to me, "Get up." When I got up, he looked at me, and I didn't know what was going on. I took off my watch and, I don't know, I thought that perhaps this might help me. He took my watch and then he hit me on the head once, twice, and there was blood flowing down my face. I had the feeling that he was in some kind of a dilemma, and then he said, "Get away from me, get away from me. Go into the cell," as if, well, I don't know. There was some force that stopped him from killing me, because -- well. Then over there, I don't know, the people who were in the cell, they helped me a bit because I couldn't breathe, either because I was so upset, because he had jumped on my chest. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Does the name Dikan say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Dikan, yes, it does. That was a Croat. He was also captured. He was from Slavonski Samac, in the Republic of Croatia, and he had been taken prisoner. He happened to be in Samac in a cafe at night. And when they saw that he was a Croat, well, they put him in the camp anyway, and they beat him a lot. I know that once when I was interrogated myself at the police station, we heard -- or, rather, I heard somebody firing in the Territorial Defence Staff, firing shots. I didn't see it, but I heard it, because it's just across the road, close by. Then Simo Zaric, who interrogated me, called up to see who had been doing the shooting, and he was told that it was Lugar, who had killed Dikan. I told you who Dikan was, and I think his sons were in the ZNGs, and so they took special care to beat him. I know Simo Zaric called up Blagoje Simic at the time and said, "That idiot," meaning Lugar, "has just killed a man." And according to the flow of the conversation, Simo Zaric with Blagoje Simic, I understood that Blagoje was asking him whether anybody had seen it happen. The answer was that at least 50 people had seen it. I know that Simo called Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic and said, "These idiots are going to kill people, and they've already killed one man, and the army has to come to save the day." Then I know that Simo left, whether he went to a factory in Samac, or Utva, or Hrana-Produkt, where Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic was located. Anyway, the army did send trucks that day; and most of us, the majority, were transported to Brcko in that truck to the barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, Mr. Tihic. Sorry. I want to come to this later. Could you please list for us the detention facilities you were aware of at that time in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: When I was in Bosanski Samac, then the Territorial Defence Staff was used and the police station building. That was turned into a sort of camp for prisoners or, rather, for citizens. It was the citizens who were incarcerated there. I know that later on, there were camps in the secondary school, the technical school, the primary school, in Crkvina, which is a village near Samac, in a warehouse there of a company called Bosanka. I know that there's another camp in Zasavica, a whole Croatian village that had been emptied of inhabitants, and they used it to put up Bosniaks and Croats there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it seems that the Prosecutor has changed topics and is now dealing with the detention centres. I would like you to shed some light on a small detail, please. I was listening to you when I was reading your statement, and I note that this Lugar -- on paragraph 44 of your statement, you seem to be saying that this Lugar is part of the Grey Wolves. Then in paragraph 52 of your statement, you say that he was one of Arkan's men. So does this mean that Arkan's men and the Grey Wolves is one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say for sure whether he was in the Grey Wolves or one of Arkan's men. When we happened to meet them, then if you dared look at anyone, because usually you'd have to put your hands behind your back and lower your head, look down, anyway, he was a man who spoke the Ekavian dialect, he was in those special units. Now, which unit he actually belonged to, or some third unit, I really can't say. I didn't know all those insignia. I couldn't recognise all the insignia that they wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in addition to what you said in your statement, you are saying that you do not really know which unit Lugar belonged to, whether it was the Grey Wolves, Arkan's men, or Unit X. You're not 100 per cent sure which unit he belonged to; is this it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the document 65 ter number 1553 to be shown on the monitor. This is an order of Public Safety Station, Bosanski Samac, signed by the witness Stevan Todorovic. The witness Stevan Todorovic is deceased some years ago, just for the information of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, could you read this and comment on this order?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: "In keeping with the law governing internal affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I hereby order ..." -- or, rather, "In compliance with," et cetera. "1. It is forbidden for three or more Muslims or Croats to congregate in public places, gather together in public places. "2. Any such grouping should be first warned; and if the offence is repeated, the participants should be apprehended and arrested. "3. For carrying out this order, the commander of the military police platoon and the commander of the public safety station are personally responsible. "Head of the Public Safety Station, Stevan Todorovic, Engineering." So that was a well-known order and it was applied. When Muslims were buried, for instance, you couldn't have a funeral procession. You could just have two or three men attending the funeral and burying the deceased. There were no send-offs or religion rites observed. They didn't allow that either, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to have this document moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P673. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I would like to come to another location. You told us shortly that you have been removed from Bosanski Samac. Could you please let us know where you have been brought?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They took almost all of us. Just five or six people remained. They took us to the military barricades in a place called Brcko, which is about 55 kilometres away from Bosanski Samac. That's where we were. We arrived there and they searched us again. They took away any items we had remaining. If anybody had a watch, a ring, or a wallet, they confiscated that, and put us into a cell. I and Dragan Lukac and Osman Isarevic [phoen] were put into a separate room because they said we were extremists. They put handcuffs on us, and that's how we spent the night. But, generally speaking, the treatment towards us in the barracks was far better than it had been in Bosanski Samac, because they didn't beat us. You were allowed to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You have not been beaten. Have you been threatened by someone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases of that kind when the Chetniks turned up. I remember on one occasion, you know, the way they were dressed with the fur hats and the skull-and-bone emblem and the beards. They threatened to kill us, and then some other groups would turn up. Whether they were Arkan's men or -- well, I don't know how this person introduced himself. But, anyway, the soldiers didn't allow them to enter, and they didn't allow them to beat us, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one small detail. You were talking about the Chetniks, notably something I'm interested in. You're telling us they had very long beards. We've seen a number of videos and photographs on this. But before these events, before 1992, were there people with very long beards already, or did this appear with the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please believe me when I say, I was wondering when they managed to grow all those long beards, because before, there weren't people with long beards. This was linked to the Chetnik movement of the day, led by Draza Mihajlovic, which was an infamous movement. You might see artists wearing beards, perhaps some painter or other, or perhaps a composer; but ordinary people didn't wear beards, especially not the long, unkempt beards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're also wondering how these beards grow so fast. I really wonder, myself. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, did you realise a kind of cooperation between the JNA and paramilitary units in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure it existed in one way or another. I don't know. They entered the barracks, and they would talk to us, threaten us, said they'd kill us all. I think there was cooperation, generally speaking, between the JNA and those various units. It couldn't have been otherwise, because how else would they have been allowed to enter the barracks, unless there was a tacit agreement for these paramilitary units to enter and unless there was cooperation? How would they enter the barracks otherwise? The barracks was a place where you weren't allowed, where entry was prohibited. You weren't allowed to photograph, you had to show your ID card, special security, let alone somebody being allowed to enter with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that time you have been asked to give a television interview?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in Brcko, I was asked to give an interview for television, and I was supposed to go to Bosanski Samac. Although I didn't feel like going, I had to go there, to Bosanski Samac, I mean. First of all, they took us to our houses so that we could have a bath, put on a decent suit to look decent and clean; and then I went to see Simo Zaric's office, where the interview was conducted in the presence -- apart from the journalists and cameramen and crewmen of TV Novi Sad, the other person there was Stevan Todorovic, who was the chief of the police station. Simo Zaric even conducted the interview, and Captain Crni came in, and other people came in from time to time. They asked me who had given the coordinates for the shelling of Samac to the Croats, and I said, "I had absolutely no idea," which was true. Then he said, "Bring him to me after the interview. I'll talk to him." So I made a statement in the only way I could, given the circumstances, in the way I had to. I know that at the end, Stevan Todorovic asked me to say that nobody had beaten me, and I did make that statement, I complied. I said that none of the Serb policemen had beat me from Bosanski Samac, and that was taped onto the interview. I said that I wasn't beaten by the Serbian police force of Samac, but by the other people who came -- but it was the people from Serbia. But they didn't notice the difference. They didn't notice the distinction I made. And after that, they returned us to Brcko. I can give you the details, if you want to hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show a short clip about this interview. We have it in our files. It's 65 ter number 6049 [Realtime transcript read in error "6449"], and please have a specific look on the left eye of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Please tell me frankly, what is your impression, Mr. Tihic, of the present authorities of the territory of the Serbian ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you speak louder? The interpreters are having a hard time hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. [Voiceover] "Mr. Tihic, let tell me frankly, what is the impression of the present authorities on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina, or rather, the Serbian police towards the Muslim people, yourself, and all the other citizens? But, please, be completely frank." "Well, as to the attitude of the Serbian police, members of the Serbian police themselves towards me personally, I didn't have any problems. I can say that they treated me fairly, properly." "Has the Serbian police force harmed anyone here?" "To the best of my knowledge and information, not one Muslim was killed. The policy of the party, especially that of President Izetbegovic, was that we must not get ourselves into a situation that becomes subordinated to any of the parties and that they merely execute their orders. And I remember that at one meeting, the SDA president from Derventa Brod said that the Croatian side provided weapons, equipment, and everything, and tried to set up a sort of staff and a joint commander where everybody would have to follow their orders. I know the president said then, 'Well, regarding equipment and weapons, take it, but without conditions. No joint commands, no joint uniforms, and so on. If someone wants to give them to you, fine, but without dragging you into their hierarchy.' Now, this issue was broached then in Bosanski Samac some 20 days ago or a month ago; I mean the idea of forming a joint Crisis Staff, as I've already said. When I attended the meeting, a meeting that was convened, I didn't know that that was on the agenda. But when I arrived ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, do you remember, is this the interview that you gave?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if, during this interview, also other detainees have been interviewed, and where were they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were interviewed, and I know that Izet Izetbegovic was there, and Alic, Omer as well, I think Safet Mihajlovic [phoen], and so on. And they were somewhere in the building, but we weren't able to contact each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have detainees been hidden, giving the interview only by voice, not shown on the television, because of their injuries?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I came from Brcko with Omer Alic and Safet Hadzialijagic, and Izet was in Samac. They were taping us separately, and I know that they would try and position the camera to hide the bruises, and that they put sunglasses on Izet. They filmed Omer in profile as well to avoid showing the injuries he had on his face. Well, it was shameful for the journalists because, well, the journalists felt ashamed because he saw what they looked like, what we looked like. Then he asked me to tell him quite frankly whether anybody beat us, whether anybody had suffered, and things like that. But who dared speak sincerely? Everybody knew what would happen if I had been sincere and frank. They would have killed us straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, like everyone else, I looked at this video. I noted that there was a cup of coffee in front of you. So were you offered a cup of coffee or was it there just, you know, to look good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, like the suit I was wearing, the cup was there to make it look as if it was a normal interview. Who placed the coffee cup there, I don't know. It was already there. There was the cup and there was the coffee inside the cup. It was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to have this video moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I was informed that the transcript of this video has the wrong number. Instead of having 6049, it has "6449." This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor ought to tell us when this interview was filmed and on what television station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, was this video broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have to search it. The originator is unknown, and this video was seized on the 11th December 1994. It's from the Videotape "Genocide, Bosanski Samac." It has been admitted into evidence in two other cases, and this is -- on the Milosevic case, it had Exhibit number 608, tab 12. In the case of -- in the Bosanski Samac case, which is IT-95-9/2, it was Exhibit number P16/A. This is the information I can give you from our documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as you know, was this interview broadcast? Did other people see it and talk to you about it? Because the Prosecutor is not giving us much of an answer. He says that it has been admitted in other cases, but we would like to know whether it was broadcast. Do you know this; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know it was broadcast on two occasions through Television Novi Sad, which has a programme in Bosanski Samac. It has a good signal and can be seen loud and clear. The locals told me that there was a problem with the electricity, which was down once when it was first broadcast, and it was broadcast again so people could see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you give us an approximate date, the date it was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was the very next day and the following day. So for two days in a row was when it was broadcast. I can make a guess and say that it was sometime around the 27th or 28th of April, perhaps, thereabouts, when it was broadcast. I can't be certain, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P674. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, after Brcko, have you been moved to another detention facility; and if so, could you let us know which one?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: From Brcko, we were transferred. After the attack on Brcko, that same night we were awoken by the explosion, all the windows were shattered, and the bridge linking Brcko to Croatia was destroyed. That same day -- or, rather, the following day, we were transferred to Bijeljina, to the barracks there. It was the Fadil Jahic Spana Barracks in Bijeljina, and we were exposed to all the abuse and mistreatment there, too, the beatings and so on. They particularly selected me. I had to wash toilets full of excrement. I had to clean it up with my hands, and they said wherever it was dirty and yellow, that it should be white, sparkling clean. But they didn't provide me with any brushes or anything, so I had to clean it with my bare hands. They would beat me, ask me to clean up the mess. Then an order came, telling me to go back to the room that the people from Samac were incarcerated in, the prisoners. Then they called us out, several of us out by name, and they ordered us about turn, to march forward, and we reached a helicopter. The helicopter transported us to the Batajnica Airport near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before we come to Batajnica, do you know if one of the guards recognised you from the television interview you gave, part of which we have seen a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, one guard did recognise me, and he said, "There's the man who was on television." I understood from that, that we were depicted in a negative light as people who had committed crimes. The policeman who recognised me took me to that toilet and asked me to clean up the mess there and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When and how have you been transported to Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: From that group of people from Samac, there were 50 of us. Five or six of us were selected and we were transferred there. We were brought to the helicopter, and we had some blindfolds over our eyes, but we could see if we looked underneath the blindfolds, and saw that there was a sort of coffin in the middle and that there were some letters on it. And as far as I had understood, it was a Serb soldier who had been killed, and his name was Vuk or Vukmirovic, something like that. Izet Izetbegovic was in the helicopter already, and Dr. Miroslav Keracic, and Benko Dragicevic -- or, rather, Ante Dragicevic, Benko's father, was there, the chief of the Samac police station, before the war, that is. They were in the helicopter and we were handcuffed. This one, well, paramilitary special had a black cap; and as the helicopter took off, he wanted to throw us out of the helicopter. However, another person who was there in the helicopter in civilian clothes did not allow him to do that. And later on, I got to know this other person. He was some security chief at the airport. And when we reached Batajnica Airport, we went through the standard procedure; that is to say, we were thrown out of the helicopter and beaten straight away, thrown into the lorry, the Pizgauer type. We were brought to a room -- well, a cellar, really; no windows, just a lamp hanging from the ceiling, one bulb hanging from the ceiling. Then, again, we were mistreated, beaten, Chetnik songs were sung. There was a picture of Draza Mihajlovic on the wall there. And in the morning, when we had to go to the toilet, we had to go and kiss Draza Mihajlovic's photograph and say, "Good morning, General," first. And on one occasion, a Croat turned up subsequently there, and he didn't know that he had to kiss -- where he had to kiss -- that he had to kiss Draza in the mouth. The policeman beat him up and said, "Draza is not a homosexual. Why are you kissing him on the lips?" Anyway, we were mistreated. We couldn't sleep. They kept calling us out and interrogating us know beating us. There are a lot of details that I could tell you. I don't know how detailed you want me to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. Could you please shortly let us know where Batajnica is? Where can we find it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Batajnica is a military airport close to Belgrade, probably the largest such military airport in the country. We were transferred there. Initially, we did not know we were at the Batajnica Airport. They tried to conceal that fact from me. I believe that we were in the cellars of an infirmary. Once, since we were badly beaten up, they brought a doctor, I think, from Zadar, a female doctor. And from the conversation we had with her, we concluded that she worked upstairs. There were some good soldiers who would not allow them to beat us up, who would bring us a doctor. I remember one, Aco Ilic, a good, kind person. When he was in charge during that shift, nobody was supposed to beat us up. There was another person from Slankamen who would also not allow mistreatment, but there were some reserve military personnel of advanced age. They were the worst. They would beat us most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember if you had to give another television interview at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had to. One day, they told me to conduct an interview. Miroslav Lazanski, a well-known commentator, conducted that interview. There were military there, there were cameras, and he asked me about us driving the Serbs out of Sabac, and I answered, "No, they drove us out." Then he asked me about us driving the Serb policemen from the police station, and I said, "No, that's not correct. Out of the 18 policemen there, 12 were Serbs." So he saw me giving opposite answers than expected. He took a look at his paper and cast a glance in the direction of a military policeman who was there, and he threatened, "Just you wait. After this interview, you'll get your comeuppance." That journalist finished the interview with me; and while I was getting up, the military policeman hit me on the head, but the other military policeman would not allow him to continue beating me, and they brought me back to the cellar. But from that interview onwards and from Izetbegovic's interview and Mr. Dragicevic's interview, who also gave a statement, they edited a broadcast to the effect that we had killed Serb children. And after the broadcast of that programme, the next day a policeman came and almost killed us with beating, because they saw it on TV. They brought this broadcast in the context of and connection with some atrocities that had allegedly occurred in Bosanski Brod. Of course, in Bosanski Samac, there was no such thing. But they edited the footage in such a way to induce such an impression, and this was the cause for the military policeman to beat us so much subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you been brought to another detention facility after Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In Batajnica, I was from the 3rd to the 27th of May, 1992, and then we were transferred to the military camp Sremska Mitrovica. There, we were detained with the people from Vukovar. It would be enough, in terms of suffering, just to be in and received at Sremska Mitrovica, and that suffering would last us a lifetime. When we were admitted into the Sremska Mitrovica camp, we were beaten naked from 3.00 to 6.00 in the morning. I had some surgical scars, having been operated on, on my hip, and I asked them, "Don't hit me there," but they especially hit me exactly there. I would pass out, then they would bring me back into consciousness, then continue beating me. I lost consciousness a couple of times during that period of torture, until 3.00 in the morning. Suddenly, there was silence, and Captain, as we called him, Blue Six - later on, I found out that he was the chief of KOS, a Croat who remained in the JNA - he asked us whether anybody had beaten us. I said, "No, nobody," because I was in the presence of the person who had beaten me. That person demanded that I strip. When I stripped, he could see redness on my skin. He asked me, "What's your profession?" I answered, "I'm a lawyer," and he said, "Shame on you. You're a lawyer, and you are lying." I said, "No, these are bruises from Batajnica." I could not admit that they were beating me there. I know that some other people told Captain Blue Six that we had been beaten in Batajnica; but as soon as he left, they continued beating those people. The Captain Blue Six brought a medical doctor with him. She gave us some powders, some pills. She could not believe the blood pressure reading that I had. But it was incredible. It was inconceivable that anyone could survive such torture. There were five or six of us. Later on, I found out that a person named Simo, who beat us very much, after five or six days invited us to get out of the room. Of course, we had to have our hands behind our backs and with our head facing downwards. He said, "We were told that you slaughtered children, Serb children, and we beat you up. But now I see from the documents that you did not do that. I will no longer beat you." But there were others who did the beating at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you get enough food in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: There was always this problem with food. It was always insufficient. In the morning, when they would bring some tea and slices of bread, some were thinner, some were thicker, and sometimes people would scuffle because of getting a thinner slice. And if we were to argue in front of military policemen, they would take away the bread and the tea. In summertime, they would bring some pasta, macaroni, some ten, 15 pieces of pasta for the whole day, and we were hungry all the time. What was interesting, after each breakfast and after each dinner, they would beat us up regularly. Of course, there were people taken out individually during the day, but what was regular was the beating immediately after breakfast and after dinner. Of course, we had to sing Chetnik songs, and there were Chetnik songs sung all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember some titles of these Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, the standard one was "From Topola to Ravna Gora Are The Sentries of General Draza." Draza was the General Mihajlovic. Then there was a song by a Croatian pop singer, Tajci, "Let's Get Crazy Tonight, Pluck Some Croats Eyes." You know, they adapted the versus to their purposes. There was Vila Velebita. Then a Muslim girl vowed before the mosque that she loves the Serbs the best in the world. Then we were made to pray Pater Noster, et cetera. Then there was another song about a bird, a popular song. Whenever they ordered us to sing some regular folk songs, that was heaven compared to what we were made to sing otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was there also a song which was called "We Will Slaughter Muslims"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Well, the general effect of those songs were, "We will slaughter, We will kill." Those were all songs that used to be sung by the Chetniks during World War II and which were prohibited during the communist Yugoslavia time. Whoever tried to sing those songs then would be put to jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave an interview to a British television station at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. On one occasion, in the morning, the commander of the camp and came and called out Filip Karaula's name. He was the commander of the Mitnica part of the Vukovar front, and me -- he invited or called out the name of a German, a volunteer in the Croatian Army. He brought us outside. He was in the company of policemen who had electric batons, and he told us that we were supposed to give a statement to a foreign TV crew. He said, "What is important for me is to say that you are not beaten, that you have all the hygiene conditions, food, et cetera." I asked him whether I was permitted to say I had been beaten at Bosanski Samac. He said, "Whatever you like, but I would advise you against saying any such things. Your family is in Rijeka, in Croatia, but they can reach your family and take their vengeance against them." Then we gave our statements, I believe, to Sky News. I'm not sure. Of course, while we were giving those statements, the commander of the camp and the chief of the KOS, K-O-S, of the camp were present, and our statements had to be adapted and adjusted to their requirements. They gave us some clothes, they cut our hair, so that we would be presentable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We have a part of this interview, and I would like to show it to you. It is 65 ter number 1059.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "A crew from a British TV agency visited the Sremska Mitrovica camp. We are broadcasting their segment in its entirety. "Over 450 prisoners, member of various Croatian formations, the ZNG, the Ministry of the Interior, and HOS, are mostly from Vukovar currently imprisoned in Sremska Mitrovica. Among them is also a group of Muslims. We recorded the statement of Sulejman Tihic, now the president, and formerly president of SDA of Bosanski Samac. "Tihic: A group of prisoners from BH, about 60 of us, appeal to the [indiscernible] of BH, urging them to take our status, our programme into consideration. We suggested that they release from military prisons or from whatever they are, where soldiers of the JNA are stationed, to release some 25 soldiers and that the JNA should then release us from Bosnia who are in the military camp in Sremska Mitrovica. Of course, I personally sent a letter to Alija Izetbegovic in my capacity as party president. And in this capacity as president of the BH SDA, I would like to take this opportunity to appeal again for our problem and the problem of those soldiers to be solved. Just like us, like all of us, those soldiers have parents, children, brothers, sisters, and everybody's waiting to get outside of detention. I am certain that this cannot be easy for them, either, and we cannot wait for the exchange to take place." "The only person in solitary confinement is the notorious Manda, who cut the throats of Serb soldiers; and of course she is the only woman here. One of the prisoners is a former member of the Yugoslav national rogue team, Kresimir Dzalto. We also report recorded the statement of Filip Karaula, the commander of the ZNJ forces in Nemetin in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, is this the video we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the footage. It was later broadcast on Croatian Television as well. My mother and my wife for the first time learned that I was alive. They were stationed in Rijeka, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to move this video into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When was it taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Give me a second. It was taken the 6th of December, 1994. It was seized at that time. I can give you, if you are interested, the exhibit number in the Bosanski Samac case. It is P17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P675. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could I please know how much time is left for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much. Registrar, please. I believe you probably have something between ten and 15 minutes left, but I will let you know. Please proceed, and the Registrar will let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to have a document shown on the monitor. Sorry, the Registrar has to do two things at a time. The document is number 1581. This a news article from the newspaper 'Borba' dated the 15th of August, 1992, and entitled "Ordinary People Remain," and the accused is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, do you remember this article?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this article. I gave this interview the day following the day I was interviewed by the 'Vis News' from England. So the first interview on TV was the 11th or the 12th, and then this article print interview was the day afterwards for 'Borba.' Military policemen showed me and brought me a copy, and I then took it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: There it said that Bosanski Samac was a very comfortable prison. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I do not agree. A prison cannot be comfortable. I told you, there were nine of us in a cell which is 1 metre 20 by 1 metre 80, with a single bench where we sat and slept.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is saying that this prison was Bosanski Samac Prison, but this is Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I apologise. It was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We will give it an exhibit number. This article will get an exhibit number. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P676. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, how long did you stay in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: From 27th of May to the 14th of August, when the exchange took place, this is the period while I was in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can you please show the document 1597 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, could you please tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate that we received after the exchange at Nemetin, near Osijek, from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. I was exchanged together with the captured people from Vukovar. This was an agreement between Panic and Gregoric, between Croatia and Serbia, all for all. And since were in that camp, we were exchanged as well. I received this certificate along with other detainees. But, here, there is this mistake that I was in Mitrovica from the 18th of April, 1992, to 14th of August, 1992. I was captured in Bosanski Samac on the 18th of April, and I was in Mitrovica from the 27th of May until the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you for letting us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have moved into evidence this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P677. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, could you please now tell us when you were exchanged, how was the procedure when you left from the prison until you were released?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You see, at first, we lived in uncertainty as to whether the Bosnia detainees would be released at all. Twenty-four hours prior to the exchange, of course, we had to clean up all the premises, the rooms, to fold neatly the mattresses that we slept on, to put our personal effects in order. These were the preparations for the exchange. On the evening of the 13th, we -- they started calling out our names to emerge from those rooms into the center of the camp. They would group us there. Then we -- our neighbours would be called out to go somewhere else. Then they were calling our names to get us on board buses. There were 15 buses, I think. At the entrance to the bus, policemen were standing and would slap people boarding the bus once or twice. And trying to avoid being hit with a baton, I did not see where I was going and I missed the step. I grabbed his - a policeman who was standing on the second step - his rifle, to stabilise myself, and they construed that as an attempt to escape, to grab his weapon. I was in the corner, in the last seat in the bus, and this helped me to avoid being beaten as badly as the other passengers. We departed late in the evening, and it took us the whole day, until 6.00 p.m., to reach Nemetin, which is 150 kilometres away. We were beaten. Whenever we would stop, local inhabitants would get on board and beat us up. There was a Montenegrin on board on the bus who was drinking brandy. He would beat us. He would invite civilians to get on board and beat us. When we reached Nemetin and waiting for the exchange, the question was whether the exchange would take place or not, whether the Croats had brought all the people to be exchanged or not. A major, at one point, entered the bus and saw that he was beating us, and he said, "You stupid peasant. Can't you see that the TV is making footage of all those people? We made sure that we did not beat them for the couple of times previously so that there are no new scars, and now you are inflicting new scars on them." That person said, "Well, they're cursing my mother." The major then demanded that we raise our heads, because we had to travel with our heads between our knees and it was very painful. The major disembarked, and then the policeman hit the person nearest to him. The major re-entered the bus, and then he cursed that policeman's mother. This journey was fraught with uncertainty. We were beaten along the way, and it took very long for us to get there. Military policemen would say, "The exchange has been called off. We will kill all of you," but, fortunately, the exchange did take place. I was exchanged at Nemetin. The Croatian side must have brought all of their prisoners. The Serbs brought all their prisoners. I was met with my wife, my son, my sister. They must have probably known that the exchange would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you later have a medical examination, and what injuries did they find?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was examined in Rijeka. They did X-rays. Three ribs on the right-hand side were broken, two ribs on the left-hand side had been broken but had healed. Then the sternum, this bone between the ribs and the bone below the last vertebra, was also broken, but it healed. Afterwards, I had to undergo hip surgery, hip replacement surgery, maybe as a consequence of the torture. Stress may have induced a colon carcinoma. I had to remove that subsequently. My front teeth were broken completely, and now I have caps on my teeth because all my teeth were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you still suffer from the consequences of these injuries?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that I have put this behind me, and I don't feel any direct effects. Perhaps these recollections take a person back to those ugly times, but life does go on normally and I don't really have any special problems on account of that. I still live in the faith that there is and will be a Bosnia and Herzegovina where all ethnic and religious groups or peoples will live together and in a spirit of tolerance. After all, in all the camps that I went through, there were always people who helped, who prevented evil from taking place. I am not a person who could identify one people or nation or one group with crimes, especially us in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can only go on living that way together, on a footing of equality. That's the way Bosnia was, and that's the way it can survive only, without anyone's domination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I was informed that I have a few minutes left, so I would like to introduce some documents which I skipped. Mr. Registrar, could you please show the exhibit -- the 65 ter number 4012.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, I would like for you to comment on this. What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This would roughly be the emblem of the Grey Wolves. I remember one of those specials, as we called them, the multicoloured ones, as we called them. He came with one of these uniforms, and he said that these emblems were not right. The four letters "S" were not put right, because they have their behinds, begging your pardon, turned to one another, because they were all supposed to face each other. How else could the Serbs be united? Then he showed the emblem of his unit, where these letters were facing each other, not as if they had their backs turned to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have moved this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... be given Exhibit number P688. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The next document I would like to show has the 65 ter number 2241.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, I would like you to tell us what it is -- what it depicts.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This is the building of the Territorial Defence Staff. That's the one that has windows, and to the left is the warehouse of the Territorial Defence where we were detained, the warehouse there and this other building. On this side of the street was the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be given Exhibit number P679. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And the last document I would like to be shown on the monitor has the 65 ter number 669. This is an excerpt from the minutes of the founding session of the SAO Northern Bosnia Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tihic, I would like you to read only the last decision which you can find on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please, could you move it a bit up, because -- down, down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: There is the last decision, which I want you to read.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I see, this is a different page. It's not there yet. Is there one more page, because you said that it was on the third page, and this is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It has the ID number 4. I have a hard copy here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the proclamation of the SAO of Northern Bosnia as an inseparable state of the Federal State. "4..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: It is too fast for interpretation, and we cannot see the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Signed, Nikola Perisic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, could you please repeat this? It was too quick for the interpreters. They could not see the text.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the proclamation of the SAO, the Serb Autonomous Province of the Republic of Bosnia as an inseparable state of the federal state. "Number 4, a large number of guests and representatives asked to take the floor and made short speeches of welcome. As all the items on the agenda had been dealt with, the president of the Assembly concluded the session at 1815 hours. "President of the Assembly, Nikola Perisic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, are you aware of this decision, and can you please comment on it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am aware of it. When this decision was made, again it was a one-sided act on the part of a group of MPs of some Serbs, not all Serbs, those from the SDS and those who wanted to attend this, because this was against the Constitution. The constitutional procedure had not been applied. This is a territory of the Doboj region that is being proclaimed a Serb territory, as if did it were not inhabited in equal numbers by Serbs and Croats. So it's evident that there was -- there were equal numbers of all three ethnic groups, all three peoples: Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. But then they took it upon themselves to say that they would pass this unconstitutional act. This also contributed to divisions and conflicts, because if Serbs proclaimed the entire territory as their own, and they constitute only one-third of the population, then, of course, the other peoples cannot accept that. You can see, by the name itself, and also the other provisions are discriminatory ones, this is the standard form of decision that was made in different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and other parts, too, where not only Serbs lived, but other peoples as well. Usually, they invoked the principles that suited them. If it is a demographic majority, then they say "demographic majority." Then if before the Second World War, they were the majority, then they would invoke that principle, that before the Second World War they were a majority. They even would say things like, if there is a single Serb somewhere or a single Serb grave, that would be Serb territory. Things like that. Of course, they'd always take more than necessary, and it was quite illegal. In a way, they were in defiance of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as if they never existed. They proclaimed institutions of their own, and in that way they produced conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. What is the date of this proclamation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's not written on there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to have this entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be given Exhibit number P680. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a brief objection, Judges, in relation to what Mr. Harhoff asked. This question makes a lot of sense. It was in 1991 that this decision was passed, and this is tendentious on the part of the Prosecutor that Mr. Tihic, the witness, read only the last part of the decision, where it remains an inseparable part of the federal state. What is meant is the SFRY, rather than the FRY, which was established on the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree with the date, 14th of November, 1991? Do you agree with the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree that's when the SFRY was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer, you have concluded your examination-in-chief; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now have a 20-minute break, and resume at 20 past 12.00 and run on until a quarter past 1.00, and Mr. Seselj will begin his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I give the floor to Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, just an advise to our two speakers. Witness, could you please wait for Mr. Seselj to be finished with his question before answering; otherwise, there will be overlapping of your two voices and interpretation will be impossible. And, Mr. Seselj, please be careful also. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, as for this tragic and difficult fate that you suffered during your life, and I had occasion to read about this in your previous statements, did you ever come across persons who introduced themselves to you as volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, or Seselj's men, rather; or did other people indicate to you that they were Seselj's men? I did not find any such thing in any of your statements.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I said that I came across people who introduced themselves and looked like Chetniks, you see. You were the leader, the political leader, of that party that promoted that. No one personally introduced himself to me as a man of Seselj's, but just as a Chetnik and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, is the Serb Radical Party the only one that affirmed the Chetnik idea, either in Serbia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the political scene?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't the only one, but you did personally to a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you knew me as a Chetnik, that's how I interpret your answer. You knew me as a prominent Chetnik, but no one from amongst the people you came across introduced themselves as a man of Seselj's, and no one said that they were Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I never had any such personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Did we know each other when we studied at the law school at the University of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You're a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1951, so I don't know when you were born.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was born in 1954. I found you there at university when I got there, but never mind. You're a lawyer. You were a judge, a prosecutor, an attorney, and now you're a prominent politician. When you were called by The Hague OTP to testify as a Prosecution witness in the proceedings against me, did you find that a bit strange? Did you wonder perhaps what it was that you had to testify about against me?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I did wonder what I was supposed to testify about, and the answer I found for myself was that I could testify as to the circumstances of my stay in camps because it was part of the general political situation then in that town, in that municipality, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, I am going to make a small inversion. First, we are going to take about your camp experiences, because I must admit to you that in a way, that is what touched me the most, if I can put it that way. You, as a politician, know that there are a few associations of former camp inmates in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And, so far, quite a few of these former camp inmates published their stories, and all of them are tragic, aren't they? Do you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we're going to dwell only on what happened to you, because you could not be blamed for what was going on elsewhere; right? Do you consider me to be responsible for everything that happened to you while you were in the detention camp in Sremska Mitrovica, in the military prison in Batajnica, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You, personally? Well, the responsibility is on the side of that policy that you promoted, inter alia, national exclusiveness, the division of Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, in accordance with the regulations of the SFRY that were then in force, that it was only the military police that was in charge of prisoners; that they were supposed to provide conditions of their detention, accommodation, et cetera, and everything else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Probably that was the case. That would only be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember who at that time was the chief of the Security Service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before that, he was the chief of security of the Sarajevo Military District. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you happened to be in these prisons or detention camps, whatever we choose to call them, in addition to the military police, there were always security officers there, too, right, or the KOS, as you called them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This was in Brcko. In Brcko, there was this one Petrovic. He was chief of this security or KOS. Then also in Batajnica, I came across that major. I mentioned that. And in Sremska Mitrovica, there was this Plavi Cest, Blue Six. He said that he was from the KOS and in that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they were practically in charge of your destiny there; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, they, together with the rest of them who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's not all right, but since things happened, then let us discuss how it happened. Can the policy of an opposition party be blamed for that, or is somebody else more responsible? The closest associates of General Vasiljevic, you remembered his name, Simeon Tumanov, who was a colonel, and then later on general; then then-Colonel, later on General Branko Gajic; and General Mile Babic who was chief of the Military Security of the 1st Military District. Have you heard of these names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Tumanov, I did hear of. It's the fact that he came to Samac when the exchanges took place. I don't know the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he organised the exchanges in Samac, you know, Tumanov?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, there was a separate political party that had been established by the generals, and it was called the League of Communists, the Movement for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what the basic objectives of that party were?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I could not say now. I assume that it was the preservation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But under special conditions, their plans were topple, as they said, the nationalist leadership in Serbia and in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, Milosevic, Tudjman and Izetbegovic, to restore Yugoslavia with foreign assistance, where they would play the main role, trying to play the role of Tito. Would that be their concept?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I could not say for sure, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. When you don't know something and if you cannot confirm something, we're going to move on straight away. I'm not going to insist, and I'm not going to try to draw something out of you that cannot be drawn. However, I think that you do know that they were Orthodox communists, if we can put it that way, the security officers.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they the main communists in the army?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: As a rule, they were -- well, how shall I put this? They were in charge of the purity of the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The communist idea?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Isn't it astonishing now that these extreme or orthodox communists, as they were keeping you in prisons, demonstrated the Chetnik idea to you, and they forced you to sing Chetnik songs, and then some songs that are not Chetnik songs, that are horrible, but that seemed like Chetnik songs to you about the killings? That is the kind of thing football fans would do, right, about slaughters, killings, things like that? Would you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Those songs were sung everywhere, in all the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not denying that, but it's astounding, is it not, that before the very eyes of the security officers, songs like that were sung?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't believe it, either. I remember, when in Mitrovica, when I was cleaning up something there and I saw Comrade Tito's picture there, I was happy to see it. When I compared it to what I was going through and what people were going through, they still had Tito's picture on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they beat you all the time and forced you to sing Chetnik songs and to kiss, as you yourself said, a photograph of Draza Mihajlovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think it was a picture -- a picture drawn of Draza Mihajlovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter either way.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was their intention when they forced you to do that? You're a politician and intellectual? Was there a intention behind that? Nothing is done by chance.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I was surprised how this could happen at all and how it could permeate the JNA. And for two or three years, we believed it to be a joint army. So I was very surprised to see that the young men there had this hatred and professed this hatred just because my name was Sulejman, and they were beating me for just that reason. We brought up our children -- our children were brought up in schools. How come, suddenly, in representative prisons as the one at the Batajnica Airport, they would have a picture of Draza Mihajlovic or be singing songs like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, here's my thesis, here's what I think. They beat you without mercy and forced the Chetnik idea so that one day, you could ascribe all that to the Chetniks; whereas, it was the KOS officers or the military security services who were still hard-line communists. That's my opinion, Mr. Tihic. Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, there were different combinations, different things were going on. I think, in the JNA, there were people who tried to protect us. There were officers like that, I remember, regardless of ethnicity, and I'm sure there were those who set out following the nationalist movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, those who tried to protect you did so individually, of their own will, because they were good people; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, probably they were good people, but they should do that even as a course of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you think that General Vasiljevic did not know what was being done to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, they had to know, as the chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the chief of the Security Service, which is a higher level than intelligence. It's counter-intelligence, as it was called previously. So you agree that he must have known about all of it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and not overlap. We can't hear them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and he didn't lift a finger to prevent it, did he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak slower, please. Mr. Seselj, do not speak so loud. The interpreters are having a difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic, a number of persons were enumerated who, together with him, allegedly took part in the joint criminal enterprise, and the media published this in Bosnia, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, just on the basis of what the media said, I couldn't mention all the names, but I know they were in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there are many high-sounding names above them, including Aleksandar Vasiljevic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't really remember. Possibly, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in one of the indictments raised against me, there is no mention of Aleksandar Vasiljevic, but I assume you don't know about that. Anyway, don't you find it strange that The Hague Tribunal and OTP never accused General Vasiljevic for taking part in war crimes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about any of that, really, to tell you the truth, and what guided the Prosecution and so on and so forth. I know that there are many people that perhaps might -- should have been taken to task and brought to court, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When we look at how the prisoners of war were treated, then he is the most responsible?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, and his superiors, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was just the minister above him. There was no superior officer above him.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Wasn't there the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, he was the chief of the Security Service of the Ministry of Defence, which was above the General Staff. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you about hierarchy and structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you know that Kadijevic was Defence minister?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you know that The Hague Tribunal and the OTP, on several occasions, brought in Vasiljevic as a Prosecution witness in other trials?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, the OTP knows that full well, but let's not dwell there. We'll move on. You said, on several occasions, that an aggression had been launched against Bosnia-Herzegovina. By whom?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina was launched by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how can the JNA launch an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina when at that time, BH was a component part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, because the JNA was working for Greater Serbian policies and politics, and it was under those instructions that they acted, that they launched an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. The JNA corps were stationed there, five of them, in fact, five corps. There were units there that were withdrawing from Slovenia and the units withdrawing from Croatia corps. And the JNA was working for that Greater Serbian project, and they used weapons to arm the Territorial Defence and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, that is a political slogan, and I assume that you're fully conscious of that yourself, that the JNA was working to promote Greater Serbia. The JNA wanted to preserve and retain Yugoslavia, and since it wasn't able to retain Slovenia, it wanted to preserve the other republics. And when it was unsuccessful in keeping the whole of Croatia, it wanted to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian Montenegro, and Macedonia within Yugoslavia, right? Never did anybody from the JNA ever mention Greater Serbia; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Not officially, but the RAM plan, R-A-M plan, if you remember that, was, in fact, a project for Greater Serbia, and that was a JNA plan, an army plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, nobody ever saw that plan, and the plan is a pure invention, fabrication pursued by The Hague Tribunal. You've never seen it either; right? They were duped.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't see it subsequently, even when you became a high-ranking officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I never dealt in military matters at all for me to have been able to see it, especially with what happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we're serious people, so when we give statements in serious places, we must be careful what we say, and the things we say must be based on certain grounds. But never mind, let's move on. I'm now going to go through several of the things in your statements made here today, and then we'll have a chance of going through all the different topics in due course. But, anyway, you said that on the 17th of April, Samac was attacked; right? How could Samac have been attacked, because over there you had the JNA, and it had the 17th Tactical Group deployed there; right? They had formed the 4th Detachment, which was supposed to be a Territorial Defence unit, but under the control of the JNA; am I right there? So it was officially the Territorial Defence formed by locals, but under the strict jurisdiction of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It wasn't Territorial Defence; it was a unit within the composition of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, you know that in case the JNA conducted operations in a certain area, that all the units of the Territorial Defence came under the command of the JNA, and that was according to the concept of total national or all people's defence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical, when it comes to an external enemy, an external foe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, tell me, why would they attack Samac if they were already in Samac and had control of the situation there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they attacked the town of Bosanski Samac, the town proper; and they wanted to take full control over the town, in my opinion, over that area, the bridge, to replace the elected powers in authority, and to hand it over to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, there was no attack?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They wanted to secure that famous corridor linking up the area with Serbia, because Samac was a essential, geographically speaking, and also because there was the bridge there and the port there and the railway there, and the border in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there was the danger of the Croatian forces entering Bosnia through that corridor?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what the Serb side said, that Bosanski Brod could repeat itself and that Croatian forces could cross over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They'd already crossed over at Bosanski Brod; right? Do you know about village of Sijekovac, in which the Croatian forces from Croatia proper committed great crimes against Serb civilians, where over 100 civilians were killed? Have you heard of Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the crimes, but I don't know who perpetrated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the information tells us that Croatian forces came across the Sava River from Croatia; nobody else. Muslims weren't committing crimes at that time, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and speak one at a time. Thank you. It's impossible to translate at this rate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, may I give you a good piece of advice. If you look at the screen, you will see that there is text coming in as we speak. I hope that you have the screen open that shows the transcript. May I suggest that you do not answer the questions until you have seen the cursor stop, because that is the time when the translation has been made and the text has gone through. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, as we were saying, there could be no attack because there was no conflict in Sabac; right? Quite simply, the JNA had left with its vehicles. With all its military equipment, it had gone out onto the streets.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They entered Bosanski Samac without permission from the authorities and without their knowledge, indeed. They started shooting first of all up into the air and then targeting certain facilities which were set fire to, and they disarmed the existing police force. They entered into all the public buildings and powers and authorities [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they had previous information, which was correct, that you had already set up a command for the town and a Territorial Defence detachment made up of 212 members which were exclusively Muslims. There was just six Croats, and all the rest were Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That was a proposal with a list of Muslim Bosniaks who had reported and wanted to be part of the Territorial Defence of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you had, as you said, 50 automatic rifles, you had weapons, you had some hunting weapons, and about 200 kilometres of explosives; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Fifty automatic rifles, I said, and I said that we had handed that over to the Territorial Defence Staff. The rifles, well, they didn't manage to hand them out. They were seized when the JNA entered Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that Territorial Defence of yours was illegal, wasn't it, because you were working pursuant to instructions from the political leadership from Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't illegal and unlawful. The Staff of the Territorial Defence was a constitutional category and therefore legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean the Staff that you set up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, not that we set up. It was the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence that appointed Marko Bozanovic, and also Alija Fitozovic as the chief, and the other person was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On what legal basis was the command for the town of Bosanski Samac appointed? It wasn't a command for the town, a municipal command?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, on the document the OTP showed us, it said "Town Command." Well, that's what it said, "Town Command," but, in fact, these were people who were concerned about their future and, therefore, wanted to see that within the legal institutions, units be established. So they put their names down to become members. The Croats and Serbs were supposed to give several thousand people like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Territorial Defence units could have existed and could exist only in cooperation with the JNA; they could not -- Territorial Defence units could not exist without the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. The Territorial Defence came under the authority of the republic, and the JNA was under the authority of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, that was the case until 1987. In 1987, that was changed. That means several years before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic --
