utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know all the provisions very well, but I know that the Territorial Defence came under the republics, at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When an expert like this tells you that in 1987, Mr. Tihic, the General Staff of the JNA was renamed the General Staff of the Armed Forces, and the Presidency of the SFRY took over the Command of the Territorial Defence and not only the JNA, and it was pursuant to an order from the Presidency of the SFRY that in 1999, they took over the weapons from the depots and warehouses of the Territorial Defence, because the SFRY Presidency concluded that at the proposal of the General Staff of the JNA, that it was too dangerous, that the Republican leadership should have such strong powers over the Territorial Defence and the armed forces should be united. So you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember all these details, as you call them. I do know that the JNA took over the weapons from the Territorial Defence depots. I know that an order like that arrived. Now, who issued the order, whether it was the Presidency or the Ministry or whoever, the Staff, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the press published articles saying that it was pursuant to an SFRY Presidency decision.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that there are documents about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The OTP have all those documents, but, unfortunately, during the proofing sessions, they didn't show them to you. But never mind. We've just observed the way in which the JNA took over control of Samac, and you said that a mass crime had been committed in Supina [as interpreted]. But I think these were only rumours, because it was investigated during the Samac group trial, Blagoje Simic et al, and nothing was proved. No traces of a crime were found, no bodies, nothing; nor was it established who the people were who could have been killed there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, all that's been proved and shown. The crime was committed before the eyes of hundreds of people in that camp over there, in the Bosanka factory warehouse, and we do know who the people were who were killed and how long the liquidation lasted. That's what I can tell you. Now, the bodily remains of those people over there were buried. The fact that they had been buried and cannot be uncovered is another matter. But the crime did take place, and both Serbs and Bosniaks and Croats and everybody can tell you about them. So there's no point in denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come The Hague Tribunal wasn't able to prove that that actually did happen?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it did prove it. It did show that it happened, because there were people on both sides -- on all three sides who saw it take place. It was public liquidation in front of the camp inmates, 16 people, 18 people, or however many. There are the names and surnames of the people there, so don't try and deny that. That's something that is very well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm just asking you. I'm not denying anything. I'm expecting an answer, because as you know, I wasn't there and didn't see anything with my own eyes. But never mind, let's move on. You said that the conflict would never have arisen had there not been intervention from outside, mostly from Belgrade -- or, rather, from the Serb side and the JNA. However, I'm sure you know just how much the Croats in your municipality arm themselves and how much weapons they receive from Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I said that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the conflict would never have arisen if the Bosnian Serbs and Croats and Bosniaks were asked, and that the conflicts through history occurred when there was interference and meddling from the surrounding parts, not only the Serbs. Conflicts occurred during world wars, and regional conflicts for that matter as well. Specifically speaking, when we're talking about this last war, there was more intensive interference and meddling on the part of the Serbs. I don't want to deny that there was interference on the Croatian side, but Serbia was more intense in that because Serbia had the army. It had the JNA, and that's why the Serbs behaved like that. Might is right. They had might behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, what could have been the role of the JNA, except to preserve Yugoslavia? The JNA had no other role, did it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think that in a way, more or less, it was included into the project of the creation of a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's just what you think. You have no proof or evidence of that. Mr. Tihic, you never heard that any of the Serbs strove and advocated a Greater Serbia, except for me; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you stated your views loud and clear and advocated that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm doing so today, too.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe other people didn't do it as officially and loudly as you, but they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I've never heard of anybody else saying things like that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you were the most consistent in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If others ever spoke about that, I did not hear them.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, they were working on accomplishing this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred when the three national parties started disagreeing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, not after that. Those parties were the least to be asked about anything, or Bosnians the least of them all. We wanted to avoid conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You declared yourselves as Muslims, and those outside wanted you to change your label into "Bosniaks," somewhere in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that was not the way it was. "Bosniaks" is an ancient term. We reinstated it. It used to exist for hundreds of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, "Bosniaks" is a label for all people who lived in Bosnia, and since I was born in Bosnia, I'm as much a Bosniak as you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is lagging behind by at least three questions and three answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will slow down. Hopefully, we will manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do I have the equal right to call myself "Bosniak" as you do? Do you know I was born in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know that you were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, maybe from Herzegovina, maybe you were born even in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo. I would know where I was born.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think that you came from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was born in the maternity ward of the Sarajevo Hospital. Do I have the right to call myself a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Everybody has the right to call themselves what they like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This right does not entail ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: "Bosniak" is an ethnic affiliation, but not an affinity towards a certain territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the question was: This only was reinstated in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We have hundreds of years of tradition of using that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But people denoted by this term were not considered as a nation. Your President Alija Izetbegovic, for decades, he declared himself as a Serb of Muslim religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, for decades, he could not have declared himself as a Muslim. This was not allowed. People either had to declare themselves as Serbs, Croats, or without ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fine. You said that the JNA organised the 4th Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group, and you mentioned that there were Muslims in that detachment as well. Did the JNA want all the Muslims to get involved into the composition of those detachments, those who were able-bodied and those who were subject to national service?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that they selected people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in Bosnia, why did the JNA want to carry out mobilisation, and that call-up was heeded mainly by the Serbs; Croats, almost none of them; and Muslims, to a certain degree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This is known to me. We did not heed the call-up because we did not want to take part in the war that was ongoing and that was forthcoming. We didn't want to be part of a policy of creation of a Greater Serbia, because the JNA had profiled itself in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, three national parties, the SDA, which organised the Muslims, the Party of Democratic Action, then the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian Democratic Union, at the elections towards the end of 1990, worked together to overthrow the communist regime and to set up a coalition government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's correct. First of all, they wanted to topple the communist regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And since the election system was complicated, one had to vote separately for rosters of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims; for instance, for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They supported each other. SDS called on Serbs to vote for Alija Izetbegovic and Fikret Abdic, as their candidates; and the SDA called on Muslims to vote for Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: When it came to the election of members of the Presidency, then people voted along ethnic lines; in other words, they voted along party lines. It is true that they were called on to vote for the other groups' representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This was done so that proportional votes would be counted, and voting was done separately for Croatian, Serb, and Muslim candidates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the ties between the three national parties were so strong that they wiped the communists out of power; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They were working in concert to move -- remove communists from power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then those three parties formed a coalition government?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that government functioned all throughout the time before the outbreak of war in Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The government functioned, approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: -- towards the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992, before the referendum, when SDS members of Parliament withdrew from the Bosnia-Herzegovinian assembly and government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Until the independent referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 28th of February and the 1st of March, 1992, when the referendum took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it known to you that such a referendum, which decides on the key question of status of Bosnia-Herzegovina, could be held only pursuant to the consensus of political representatives of all three peoples?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The decision on the referendum was reached through parliamentary procedure. Most of the Serbian representatives were against. All SDS members and members of Parliament voted against the referendum, but that referendum was fully legal, pursuant to the laws and Constitution, and it was conducted as such. So it would have been better if support from the SDS were forthcoming, but they had left the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you are a lawyer. You know the Constitution of the BiH. Didn't the three peoples, the Serbs, Croats and Muslims - this is how it's stated in the Constitution, then the order of listing the peoples are changed intentionally to underline the equality - were those peoples constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, constituent peoples and equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What -- how do you ascribe the quality of being a constituent people? That means that each people is a constitutional factor, without whose will the Constitution cannot be changed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: All international organisations, the International Community, accepted that referendum as lawful. More than 64 per cent of the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted for independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, a huge number of countries of the world recognise this Tribunal as legal, although it is not. So the fact that somebody from outside recognised what you did doesn't mean that your deed is lawful, because in the West, there are fewer people who understand the specific Yugoslav theory of being a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: First of all, I think that this Tribunal is legal. It was established by the UN. The question of constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina and their equality was resolved in one manner in the communist or socialist constitution, and in another manner following the Dayton Accords. According to that then-Constitution, this referendum was legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, that referendum was not -- did not have legal effect, because the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not changed in the way that the Constitution forces.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: By that time, the Constitution had not been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it was changed afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. After independence was declared, there were certain changes to the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What I want to say is this: The status of a Constitution of people is a legal formulation which preempts majorisation, which was out-voting. It was a constitutionally-enshrined mechanism preventing one people to be out-voted by the other two people. Muslims counted 42 per cent at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbs were some 35, 17 of Croats, et cetera. But the Constitution guaranteed that two peoples would team up against the third people and impose their will on that third people. The Constitution demanded that each status issue in question in Bosnia-Herzegovina be resolved through full consent of the representatives of all three peoples; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: A referendum was not organised for the peoples to vote, but citizens, and 64 per cent of citizens voted. How many of them were Muslims, Croats, or Serbs, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is exactly what the Constitution barred. Had it been enshrining the concept of citizens, then the Constitution would not have cited which peoples were constituent people and altered the order of their mention, and that the Constitution did not speak about citizens. It recognises the notion of constituent people to prevent out-voting a certain constituent people at referendums, the same way that they voted for different candidates at elections, voting for the other groups' candidates for the Presidency, the same way a referendum was possible if a majority of Serbs were to vote for something, a majority of Muslims to vote for, and a majority of Croats to be voting for. This was the only way that independence could have been voted for?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: None of our legal instruments foresaw constituent peoples to vote. That right lies with individual citizens. All legal instruments to protect constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina were used, and the referendum decision was adopted pursuant to the laws and Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, through his question, ascertains that the referendum was illegal. This is not the first time that he is saying this, and he is repeating it again here. As a lawyer, what I would like to know from you is this: Did the Constitution allow for a referendum, notwithstanding the issue of the constituent people? Was a referendum authorised by the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, sir. It was possible to hold a referendum pursuant to the Constitution if the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to invoke it, and the Assembly did so pursuant to the effective laws, and this is how it was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, the Constitution did not permit a referendum to change constitutional provisions; isn't that correct? The Constitution laid down a strict procedure for its amendments. A referendum could not be used to amend the Constitution; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which constitutional provision provided for a referendum to be used to change or amend the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Referendum did not change the Constitution. We voted at the referendum on whether the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in favour of an autonomous, independent, sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. That referendum did not vote on certain provisions of the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Constitution was being violated, because in its initial provisions, the Constitution says that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a sovereign state - and, here, we see the constituent people are a sovereign people - is associated into the SFRY as an equal republic of the Federation. Is my interpretation good?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you give me a better interpretation of the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The Assembly adopted a decision on the referendum. The referendum was conducted pursuant to the effective legislation at the time. It was completely legal, lawful. And if somebody thought that Constitution was violated, they could have petitioned the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, claiming that such a decision was counter-constitutional. Today, we can spend the whole day discussing whether it was constitutional or unconstitutional, but I and many international legal experts, including those in the Badinter Commission, thought that this referendum was constitutional. You think that it wasn't. If somebody wants to -- felt that this was unconstitutional, they could have petitioned the Constitutional Court. Only the Constitutional Court had it within its purview to rescind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that all the scallywags that we've had occasion to contact together with the Badinter Commission, and this, the Brcko commission, et cetera, nobody entered the constitutionality of that? I'm talking about the Constitution as it was written, and I'm not discussing the opinions of those who never read that Constitution. When Muslims and Croats said that they wanted independence, and the Serbs said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you referred to the Badinter Commission, and you said "the foreigners who have not read our Constitution." What you are saying is rather an extraordinary statement. Do you believe that also, Witness, that people from the outside had not read the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Badinter Commission was an expert legal commission. They read all the constitutions, the SFRY's Constitution, the republic's constitution, and they concluded that pursuant to all the constitutions, federal or republican, the decision on getting independence could have been taken. They said this ought to be done via a referendum, and this is what they said. This commission comprised the top legal experts who were cognizant of the Constitution of the Federation and the federal republics of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You Muslims decide that you want independence; the Croats decide that they want independence; and the Serbs also decide, by way of a referendum, that they want to remain in Yugoslavia. They had lived in Yugoslavia until then, and they wanted to live in Yugoslavia in the future, too; whereas you, who want independence, you can secede, you can obtain independence. Is it clear to you that the Serbs could not allow this kind of out-voting, and that by way of out-voting the Serbs, at the referendum, you caused a bloody civil war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's not the way it was, you know. I said that the citizens voted on a referendum in accordance with the Constitution. As for all the actions that took place leading to the war, as you saw the proclamation of different kinds of Serb autonomous districts and municipalities, and the interference of the JNA, the war had already started even before this referendum, if I can put it that way. There was a state of war precisely because of this policy of a Greater Serbia that had, as its objective, to annex parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina or all of Bosnia and Herzegovina in to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, you used to be a supporter of the Belgrade declaration, and you supported the policies of Adil Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic, who wanted Yugoslavia to stay on, even a smaller Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I never supported Adil Zulfikarpasic or Filipovic's party. This was a small political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina that tried to contribute to the prevention of a war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. We were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia as a federative or confederative state in which all the republics would stay on, including Croatia, too, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Tomorrow, then, we will have an opportunity to discuss some questions of principle as well. Up until the end, we have only a few minutes left, so we'll just deal with something very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're quite right. We shall proceed tomorrow, because we've just about reached the moment when it is time to stop. Let me remind you, Mr. Seselj, that you've had 45 minutes so far. Witness, as you know, you are a witness of the Court, since you have taken the oath, and you know full well now that you cannot have any contacts with the OTP. So let me recommend that you do not discuss these matters with anyone, and we shall be happy to see you again tomorrow morning at 8.30. Rest assured, Mr. Seselj will finish his cross-examination. There might be some redirect. The Bench may also put questions to you. But, normally speaking, your testimony should be over by tomorrow. I wish you all a pleasant afternoon, and we shall meet again, as I have said, tomorrow morning at 8.30. Thank you. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
